Despite the excitement around Donald Trump’s new sanctions and even the US strikes against the Iranian island of Larak just hours ago, much suggests that Trump is not seeking a dramatic ratcheting up of pressure on Iran. According to reports Sunday, the US military hit Iranian launchers on the island to prevent Tehran from planting new mines in the Strait of Hormuz. This
items.titleTR: Trump’s try to keep the Iran war from backfiring further

slots.packetSpot: According to reports, the US military struck Iranian launchers on Larak Island in order to prevent Tehran from laying new mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The attack, whose details have not yet been disclosed, is being presented as the first known US strike on Iran since Donald Trump declared a ceasefire in July.
slots.packetTitle: The shadow of mines over Hormuz

items.descriptionTR:
President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Iran will reciprocate immediately if Washington returns to its commitments under a June 17 framework for peace talks, as pressure mounts on Tehran in the face of an economic crisis.
His comment came as two supertankers were attacked off Oman, a day after the first US-Iran exchange of fire in more than a month. One was the Saudi-owned Sidr, a very large crude carrier (VLCC) that Iran's Tasnim news agency said had “stopped” in the southern corridor of the Strait of Hormuz. The other was the Sinokor-operated Senegal Property.
Mr Pezeshkian, speaking on Tuesday at a summit of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, accused the US of breaching the June 17 framework that was supposed to lead to peace talks and the Strait of Hormuz reopening.
The framework agreement lasted less than two weeks before Washington began making “excessive demands” and failing to honour its commitments, said Mr Pezeshkian, who had signed up to it with US President Donald Trump.
I state explicitly that if the US returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action
Masoud Pezeshkian, President of Iran
“It is self-evident that the violation of the US commitments was met with an appropriate response from Iran,” Mr Pezeshkian said, without elaborating on the measures taken by Tehran.
“But I state explicitly that if the US returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action,” he added in a speech at the summit.
Washington stepped up economic pressure against Tehran following the latest flare-up between the two arch foes, with Mr Trump saying sweeping new sanctions were “kicking in really strongly”.
The exchange of fire overnight from Sunday into Monday was the first since last month, with American forces carrying out strikes on the Iranian island of Larak in the Strait of Hormuz and Iran targeting US bases in Jordan in retaliation.
US scope for diplomacy
Central Command, which oversees US military operations across the Middle East, said there was “limited, precise action” and that the strikes followed the detection of Iranian preparations to lay new sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles after Iran attacked US bases in the kingdom.
Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed, said the Iranian attacks on Gulf states and Jordan had “proven to be a failure”.
Mr Trump vowed to retaliate, telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” But he also suggested there was still scope for diplomacy, saying Iran “want[s] to meet so badly”.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, speaking as G20 finance ministers met in North Carolina, warned that those engaging with Tehran risked being cut off from the dollar-based financial system.
“I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically,” Mr Bessent said, as Washington sought international support for its campaign to sever Iran’s financial lifelines.
Iran has been gripped by an economic crisis, with the government struggling to pay wages and supply enough fuel for motorists in the face of US sanctions and a naval blockade.
In a written statement issued on Sunday, supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei called for unity and warned officials against exposing the country’s weaknesses amid fears of renewed unrest.
Long queues have formed at petrol stations in Tehran over the past week, with some closing or running dry despite a record amount of fuel being distributed in the capital.
Anger over the collapsing rial, high prices and the cost of living prompted deadly demonstrations in December and January, while petrol shortages, supply disruption and long queues have added to public anxiety over the reliability and cost of basic services.
Iran’s judiciary chief, Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei, on Monday threatened a tougher crackdown on any new anti-government protests.
“If the enemies seek to disrupt the security of the people at home and make a mistake, they can be certain that they will face a stronger, firmer and more decisive response than in any previous period,” he said.
Iran’s currency has plunged to ‌a record low this month, crossing the psychological threshold of ⁠2 million rials per US dollar, while annual ⁠inflation reached 66 per cent in July.
Central bank governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said on ⁠Tuesday he was ready to inject up to $2 billion into the foreign exchange market to calm the volatility.
“I am telling the President ⁠of the United ‌States: Iran has [foreign] currency and it has enough,” Mr Hemmati said.
“I tell the people with complete honesty that economic conditions and livelihood management have become difficult, but collapse has never happened and will never ‌happen. These claims are ⁠just psychological warfare and the dust will settle soon.”
items.titleTR: Pezeshkian leaves door open to US talks as Iran economy reels

slots.packetSpot:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran would respond immediately if the United States returned to its commitments under the June 17 peace-talk framework. Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Pezeshkian accused Washington of violating the framework.

The statement came at a time of renewed escalation in tensions between Iran and the United States. US Central Command reported that a limited and precise operation had been carried out near Larak after preparations to lay new naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz were detected. It was announced that Iran had targeted US bases in Jordan and that Jordan had intercepted eight Iranian missiles. It was also reported that two supertankers had been attacked off Oman.

As Washington increased economic pressure, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said countries engaging with Iran could face the risk of exclusion from the dollar-based financial system. It was reported that fuel queues and supply shortages were being experienced in Iran; that the rial had fallen to a record low this month, surpassing the 2 million threshold against the dollar; and that annual inflation had reached 66 percent in July.
slots.packetTitle: A promise in return for renewed commitments

items.descriptionTR: North Korea and the United States could resume dialogue "at any time in the future," but direct communication cannot be confirmed, the National Intelligence Service revealed Tuesday. According to Rep. Youn Kun-young of the Democratic Party of Korea, a member of the Intelligence Committee, the NIS believes a meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un is possible. However, the agency has so far been unable to verify whether any communication has taken place betwe
items.titleTR: US-N. Korea dialogue could resume 'any time' but no signs of direct contact: spy agency

slots.packetSpot:
Democratic Party lawmaker Youn Kun-young, relaying South Korea’s National Intelligence Service briefing to the National Assembly Intelligence Committee, said it assessed that dialogue between the United States and North Korea could resume at any point in the future. According to the agency, a meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un also appears possible.

By contrast, it has not been confirmed that direct communication has been established between Washington and Pyongyang. While Trump recently said he was willing to meet Kim by the end of 2026, North Korea has remained largely silent. It was also stated that Seoul has not yet contacted Pyongyang about its proposal for multilateral talks involving both Koreas.
slots.packetTitle: Silence before a possible meeting

items.descriptionTR:
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune is aiming to introduce the death penalty for arsonists, after 12 people were killed in wildfires that swept through the northeast of the country last week.
Mr Tebboune has given the Minister of Justice until September 15 to implement the change. He was speaking at a meeting held to discuss the wildfires and revealed that a number of people had been arrested following last week's fires.
“Whoever thinks that the law will not be applied, let him know that society and justice will take their due from him," he said, according to state news agency APS.
The death penalty is in the country's criminal code for several offences, but its use has effectively been suspended since 1993. Under the current law, deliberately igniting forest fires is punishable by up to 30 years in prison, a clause which the president is seeking to change.
Last week's wildfires came after an exceptional heatwave swept across North Africa, with Tunisia and Algeria particularly affected.
Algeria's civil protection services recorded 154 wildfires across the country on Wednesday, 36 of which were in Bejaia province alone. Half of them have been brought under control.
The fatalities included five people in Jijel province, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou. Fifty-four people suffered burn injuries, including six in critical condition who are currently in intensive care, Interior Minister Said Sayoud said.
Mr Tebboune declared three days of national mourning. "It is not normal for fires to break out at the same time, like the one that broke out at one o'clock in the morning and spread quickly without any wind," he said.
Work is underway at the Ministry of Finance to calculate compensation for those who have been affected "regardless of the nature of the losses", APS quoted the president as saying.
Alternative housing is also being provided for those who lost their homes, and new standards will be implemented for building homes in forested areas, APS added.
items.titleTR: Algeria seeks introduction of death penalty for arson after fatal wildfires

slots.packetSpot:
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune called for the introduction of the death penalty for arsonists after 12 people died in forest fires in the country’s northeast. The Justice Ministry was reportedly given until 15 September to implement the change; under the current law, deliberately starting a forest fire is punishable by up to 30 years in prison. Although the death penalty remains in the penal code for certain crimes, executions are said to have been effectively suspended since 1993.

According to Interior Minister Said Sayoud, 54 people were injured in the fires; six are in serious condition and in intensive care. Five of the deaths were recorded in Jijel, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou. Civil defence services detected 154 fires nationwide in a single day during an exceptional heatwave affecting North Africa; 36 of them were in Bejaia.

According to APS, Tebboune said that some people had been detained following the fires; he declared three days of national mourning. Compensation assessments are under way for those affected, while alternative housing is being provided to people who lost their homes. New building standards are also planned for homes in forested areas.
slots.packetTitle: After the fires, a push for the death penalty

items.descriptionTR:
•	Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks
	•	Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations
A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.
The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.
items.titleTR: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash

slots.packetSpot:
The pre-match flypast over Cape Town Stadium took place before around 56,000 people. Based on a Flightradar24 estimate, the lead of two passenger-free Embraer aircraft operated by Airlink passed 12 to 14 metres above the stadium roof; the second aircraft flew through a cloud of pink powder rising from the roof as part of the display.

Airlink said the flight was conducted at about 150 knots; that it had been carefully planned and rehearsed, and carried out in accordance with safety regulations with the guidance, approval and support of the South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic and Navigation Services. The company also said it had provided flight data and black-box recordings to the authority for review. The authority has not yet commented; it was reported that it plans to issue a statement.

Aviation experts Chris Martinus and Keith Tonkin argued that the margin for error is narrow at such a low altitude. Tonkin said pilots' room to manoeuvre could be limited in circumstances such as turbulence or a bird strike, and that the flight could also set a precedent for similar displays. Stadium flypasts are not new in South African rugby: before the 1995 World Cup final between the same two teams, a Boeing 747 passed over another stadium in Johannesburg.
slots.packetTitle: At the stadium roof's edge

items.descriptionTR: DAKAR, Sept 1 - Guinea-Bissau has approved a new constitution in a referendum, provisional results showed on Tuesday, expanding presidential powers and reshaping electoral rules ahead of a presidential election scheduled for December.
items.titleTR: Guinea-Bissau approves new constitution that expands presidential powers

slots.packetSpot:
According to provisional results announced by Guinea-Bissau’s National Electoral Commission, 70 percent of votes in the constitutional referendum were in favour of the changes and 30 percent against; around 544,060 people voted. The measures ahead of the presidential election planned for December grant the president the power to appoint or dismiss the prime minister and cabinet, create or abolish ministries, and dissolve parliament in the event of a severe political crisis.

In the country, where military officers seized power in a coup last November, PAIGC boycotted the vote, saying political and institutional safeguards were insufficient. Domingos Simoes Pereira accused supporters of the referendum of trying to eliminate freedom and democracy. It was reported that some polling stations in Bissau remained largely empty, while some residents said they had not been aware of the vote or did not understand its purpose.
slots.packetTitle: The presidency’s widening reach in Guinea-Bissau

Kroenke Sports + Entertainment announced Tuesday that it will buy a controlling interest in the Los Angeles Angels from Arte Moreno in a deal that is expected to close in the first quarter ⁠of 2027.
The sale will require the approval of Major League Baseball and its owners.
items.titleTR: Stan Kroenke, owner of Arsenal and LA Rams, to buy MLB’s Angels for reported $4bn

slots.packetSpot:
Kroenke Sports + Entertainment announced that it had reached an agreement to purchase the controlling stake in the Los Angeles Angels from Arte Moreno. The transaction is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027, following approval from Major League Baseball and club owners.

The $4 billion price reported by ESPN would surpass the previous MLB sale record if completed. After Moreno, who has owned the Angels since 2003, the club could join the Kroenke Sports + Entertainment portfolio, which also includes the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche, Colorado Rapids and Arsenal.
slots.packetTitle: A new owner on the horizon for the Angels

items.descriptionTR:
•	CBS analyst was arrested in July after traffic stop
	•	Former QB has been absent from CBS duty
CBS NFL analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo has pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated and has apologized for the actions that led to his July arrest.
Romo was arrested on 23 July following a traffic stop in Wisconsin. CBS has since placed him on leave from his role as its lead NFL analyst.
items.titleTR: Former NFL star Tony Romo given driving ban and vows to ‘own my mistakes’ after OWI arrest

slots.packetSpot:
Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback and CBS NFL commentator Tony Romo entered a no-contest plea to a drunk-driving charge brought after a traffic stop in Wisconsin on July 23. According to court records, he will be unable to drive for six months; he must complete an alcohol assessment program, pay $834, and have an ignition interlock device in vehicles he uses, owns or that are registered in his name for at least one year after getting his license back.

CBS placed Romo on leave from his role as lead NFL commentator; no timetable has yet been announced for a decision on his future at the network. Romo said he was apologizing and taking responsibility. In his own words, he described how ongoing pain after multiple back surgeries led to dependence on pain medication, and how his effort to stop taking those medications led to excessive reliance on alcohol; he said he was working with doctors on his health issues.

Records released by the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office noted that Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests and that an open bottle of an alcoholic beverage was found on the passenger side of his Jeep. A deputy sheriff also said he suspected Romo may have been impaired because of red, glassy eyes and the smell of alcohol.
slots.packetTitle: Tony Romo faces his mistakes

items.descriptionTR:

	•	Winner sobbed after his shock success
Bastien Tronchon claimed victory in stage 10 of the Vuelta a España as the Frenchman edged a thrilling bunch sprint on Tuesday.
The Groupama rider was followed over the line by Magnus Cort Nielsen and Thibau Nys, who edged Wout van Aert to complete the day’s podium. The Spaniard Enric Mas retained the red jersey ahead of Primoz Roglic and Felix Gall in the general classification.
items.titleTR: Vuelta a España: tearful Tronchon claims surprise stage victory in chaotic finish

slots.packetSpot:
Bastien Tronchon's unexpected stage victory in the uphill bunch sprint in Elche de la Sierra defined an eventful day on stage 10 of the Vuelta a España. In a result reported to be the 24-year-old Groupama-FDJ French rider's first WorldTour win, Magnus Cort Nielsen finished second and Thibau Nys third; Wout van Aert was also among those who missed out on victory at the finish.

Enric Mas reached the finish with the leading group to retain the overall lead by 1 minute 18 seconds over Primož Roglič. Tadej Pogačar, who abandoned the race on stage eight, reportedly underwent surgery on his left collarbone in Barcelona; it was reported that defending his world championship title in Montreal at the end of September appeared highly unlikely, though no decision has yet been made on his return to racing.
slots.packetTitle: A surprise finish at the Vuelta

items.descriptionTR: Juventus have announced the arrival of Newcastle forward Nick Woltemade and Tottenham Hotspur midfielder Pape Matar Sarr on season-long loan deals.
items.titleTR: Juventus sign Woltemade and Sarr on loan

Juventus are adding Newcastle forward Nick Woltemade and Tottenham midfielder Pape Matar Sarr to their squad on loan until the end of the season. Sarr's deal includes an obligation to buy.

Woltemade's deadline-day loan move to Juventus has been completed. The 24-year-old Germany international joined Newcastle from Stuttgart last summer for €75 million plus up to €5 million in add-ons.

Aston Villa added 18-year-old Senegalese winger Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris Saint-Germain and 24-year-old English centre-back Taylor Harwood-Bellis from Southampton on the final day. It is reported that €55 million (£47 million) was paid for Mbaye, while Harwood-Bellis’s initial £25 million fee could rise by £4 million in add-ons.

The two transfers stand out as part of the extensive summer rebuild under Unai Emery. Villa are reported to have spent around £280 million over the summer, with that figure potentially nearing £300 million if conditions are met; they are also said to have generated more than £300 million from player sales. The club’s previous sanctions under UEFA financial rules and its settlement agreement also form part of the backdrop to this activity.

items.descriptionTR:
Britain’s Foreign Secretary has given the strongest signal yet that the government is preparing sanctions to imminently target businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Ed Miliband disclosed that the government would announce a “comprehensive set of measures” in the coming weeks as ministers seek to prevent the destruction of the prospect of a Palestinian state.
His comments, made during his first Foreign Office Questions in Parliament, have fuelled expectations that sanctions on companies and other organisations involved in the settlements are imminent.
Mr Miliband said the Israeli settlements were illegal under international law and condemned the recent issuing of tenders for construction in the E1 area of the West Bank, which he described as a long-standing “red line”.
“This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution,” he told MPs. “We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.”
Explaining the British government's toughening stance, he said that what had happened in Gaza and the West Bank “has pricked the conscience of a generation and that’s why we will act”.
His words were reiterated shortly after by Andy Burnham, making his first appearance at the despatch box as rime Minister. He reminded MPs he had said before he became PM he thought the government needed to look again at its approach to Israel. He said the E1 settlement extension and fast-tracked tender process made matters urgent.
Asked whether action should extend beyond goods to services, including mortgages, financial support and legal services provided by British companies to settlement builders, the Foreign Secretary said the government was examining its “wider economic relationship with the occupied territories”.
“We do not want British companies financing, constructing or advertising new settlements,” he said. “The work we are now undertaking is how we can stop that.”
His remarks represent the clearest indication yet of the scale of measures being considered, although the UK government has been signalling for some time that further action against settlement activity was under consideration.
Conservative MP Kit Malthouse argued that the UK’s approach to Palestine had been “an almost complete failure of British foreign policy” and it was “distressing” to witness ministers “sent out like goldfish that mouth platitudinous condemnation, promise action, only being dragged to pathetic, ineffectual steps by pressure from their own backbenchers … Is anything going to change?”
Responding, Mr Miliband said action was urgently required as the illegal settlement expansion continued.
“If you are for the two-state solution and you see it being destroyed by the facts on the ground, you must act,” he said. “And I can assure him … we are going to.”
He said the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, had recognised the need for a “step change” in Britain's approach because of the urgency of the situation.
The UK government is expected to announce the details of its package before the House of Commons begins its conference recess in just over two weeks' time.
The precise targets and legal mechanisms remain unclear. Ministers have yet to confirm whether any new sanctions would cover individual companies, financial institutions or the provision of services to settlement-related businesses.
items.titleTR: Ed Miliband signals imminent UK sanctions on occupied West Bank businesses

slots.packetSpot:
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described Israeli settlers’ violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank as “horrific” in Parliament on 1 September and said his country would make a sweeping change in policy. Miliband said he would announce detailed measures in the coming weeks; they did not want British companies to finance, build or promote new settlements.

Miliband also said the broader economic relationship with the occupied territories was being examined. In June, Britain had announced sanctions against six entities and one individual linked to financing, facilitating or carrying out settler violence.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, meanwhile, warned that if Britain took action against Israel, Israel would respond. He did not specify what the response would be; it had been reported that Israel was considering expelling diplomats.
slots.packetTitle: London draws a new line on settlements

items.descriptionTR:
Michigan Senate candidate accuses vice-president of ‘dog whistle’ and says Republican policies are true evil
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate in Michigan, has hit back at Republican vice-president JD Vance’s onslaught against him, saying it is “evil” to deprive people of healthcare and affordable groceries.
Vance, in a Monday speech that railed against undocumented immigrants, cast El-Sayed as representative of “terrible evil” and as someone who fights for “one group at the expense of others”.
items.titleTR: Democratic contender Abdul El-Sayed hits back at JD Vance over ‘evil’ taunt

slots.packetSpot:
Vice President JD Vance’s description of Abdul El-Sayed as “very, very bad” in Michigan’s Senate race has intensified the identity- and politics-laden dispute between the candidates. In a speech in Sterling Heights, Vance accused the Democratic candidate of putting one ethnic group ahead of others; he urged voters to support Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed, in turn, described taking healthcare away from workers, giving tax cuts to billionaires, raising food and gasoline prices, and dividing people for political gain as “evil.” He called Vance’s remarks a “dog whistle,” linking them to what he said were Islamophobic attacks he had faced throughout his campaign.

The dispute also brought renewed attention to El-Sayed’s earlier post about Vance’s wife, Usha Vance. While conservative commentators found the post racist and inappropriate, Usha Vance said her husband’s family had treated her warmly. El-Sayed said he preferred not to speak about spouses; he argued that Vance was rooted in a political outlook that sees some people as “more American” than others.

El-Sayed had narrowly edged Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary. In a race in which Rogers is trying to reach moderate Democrats and Jewish voters, El-Sayed said Michigan voters would defeat Rogers in November.
slots.packetTitle: A fight over “evil” in Michigan

items.descriptionTR:
Tony Graf to decide if there is sufficient evidence to try Tyler Robinson and allow prosecutors to seek death penalty
	•	Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email
A Utah judge is expected to rule ⁠on whether the ⁠man accused of killing Charlie Kirk should stand trial and whether he should face the death penalty.
Arguments were set to begin in Provo, Utah on Tuesday afternoon, after which judge Tony Graf ⁠will decide whether there is sufficient evidence to try Tyler Robinson, 23, and allow prosecutors to seek the death penalty for the murder of one of the US ⁠right’s most prominent figures.
items.titleTR: Judge to rule on whether accused Charlie Kirk killer will stand trial

items.descriptionTR: PROVO, Utah, Sept 1 - Prosecutors on Tuesday urged a Utah judge to order a capital murder trial for the 23-year-old man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, arguing that spectators only feet from Kirk were endangered, while defense lawyers said the shooting did not meet the standard for aggravated murder.
items.titleTR: Utah prosecutor in Charlie Kirk trial urges judge to allow death penalty

slots.packetSpot:
In Utah, Judge Tony Graf ruled that Tyler Robinson, who is accused of killing Charlie Kirk, will stand trial on murder charges. Robinson has not yet entered a plea; a hearing at which the indictment will be read will be held after the hearing.

Prosecutors argue that the shooting of Kirk at an event attended by about 3,000 people at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, also endangered those nearby. This claim could be decisive for an aggravated murder charge under Utah law and a possible death sentence. Prosecutors also rely on video footage, rifle and DNA evidence, messages, and anti-fascist phrases on shell casings; they also allege that the attack was politically motivated.

Defense lawyers, meanwhile, challenge the reliability of the DNA analysis and argue that the single shot endangered no one other than Kirk. The decision to proceed to trial does not mean that Robinson has been found guilty or will be sentenced to death.
slots.packetTitle: A case at the threshold of death

items.descriptionTR:
•	Kim Birrell, Maya Joint and James Duckworth advance on day two
	•	Birrell plans to spend $265,000 pay day on upcoming wedding
An elated Kim Birrell plans on paying down her mortgage after surviving a match point and a restless night’s sleep to chalk up a life-changing US Open win in New York.
The gritty Gold Coaster wore down Croatian Petra Marcinko 3-6, 7-6 (7-4), 6-3 to finally reach the second round after losing all three of her previous Flushing Meadows openers in 2023, 2024 and 2025.
items.titleTR: Australian tennis battlers savour ‘crazy’ pay days at US Open

slots.packetSpot:
It was a mixed opening day for the Australians at Flushing Meadows. Taylah Preston became the first Australian to reach the second round of the women’s singles, beating Alycia Parks 6-3, 6-3; Talia Gibson, Storm Hunter and Adam Walton exited the tournament early.

Kim Birrell left the court because of rain at 3-3 in the second-set tie-break after losing the first set against Croatia’s Petra Marčinko. Aleksandar Vukic’s five-set match against Japan’s Rei Sakamoto was also halted in the deciding set, with Sakamoto leading 4-3. Alex de Minaur was due to begin his tournament against Andrea Guerrieri.
slots.packetTitle: Australia’s uneven start at Flushing Meadows

items.descriptionTR: Niger’s military government has survived its most serious internal challenge since seizing power in 2023, after Russian paramilitaries helped loyalist forces crush last Saturday's attempted coup in the capital, Niamey. RFI spoke to an expert who explains how this episode has left General Abdourahamane Tiani’s junta weakened and more dependent on Russia.
items.titleTR: Niger coup attempt: 'Russians saved the day' analyst tells RFI

slots.packetSpot:
It was reported that Base 101 in Niamey had been seized and that attacks had been carried out on the presidential palace and state television. While Niger’s Defence Ministry described the violence as a “spontaneous outburst” in which soldiers had broken the rules, Yvan Guichaoua of the Bonn International Centre for Conflict Studies assesses that the selection of three strategic targets points more strongly to an attempted coup.

Loyal forces are reported to have later retaken the base at the airport. It is stated that Russia’s ambassador to Niger said assistance had been requested and that the Africa Corps had provided support; unnamed observer and security sources are said to have reported that kamikaze drones were used. Guichaoua believes this support may have been decisive in suppressing the uprising.

Although General Abdourahamane Tiani’s administration has remained standing, Guichaoua says Russia’s involvement could increase the junta’s dependence on Moscow and deepen the divide between the presidential guard and the rest of the army.
slots.packetTitle: Niamey’s lifeline reaches to Moscow

items.descriptionTR:
Late changes to South Africa’s team smacked of mind games, but a reinvigorated New Zealand remain in the hunt
The margins are slim in South Africa this past fortnight and not just on the scoreboard. According to aviation experts, one of the two planes flying over the stadium in Cape Town just before kick-off on Saturday came within 12 to 14 metres of hitting the top of the stand which, depending on your perspective, either ranks as highly skilled piloting or the most gratuitous of matchday stunts.
Something similar could be said, as it happens, about Rassie Erasmus’s ongoing selectorial high jinks. His initial starting XV announced for the second Test bore about as much resemblance to the one that ultimately took the field as Erasmus did to the late, great Dolly Parton, with no fewer than six of the original lineup missing. It had the desired result in terms of South Africa levelling up the four-Test series at 1-1 but was yet another example of Erasmus toying with the game’s supposed conventions.

items.descriptionTR:
The World Food Programme is to cut the number of people receiving assistance in the occupied West Bank by half owing to a lack of funding.
The "difficult decision" means 200,000 of the 400,000 people the WFP has been helping will continue to receive cash vouchers, food items, livelihood programmes or nutritional services, the UN body said. The cut is to take effect this month.
The WFP said the need for assistance in the West Bank had more than doubled since 2023, when an escalation in violence by Israeli forces and illegal settlers caused the forcible displacement of Palestinians and the disruption of livelihoods. It left more than 900,000 Palestinians food insecure.
West Bank violence has escalated further in recent months. On Tuesday, Israeli forces carried out demolitions on a farm, official Palestinian media said. In Gaza, residents told The National that Israel had launched at least 15 strikes during a special commando operation against Hamas.
Two-thirds of households in the West Bank have experienced a "significant decline in income", the WFP said, while food and fuel prices remain among the highest in the region.
￼
Rural areas have been the most affected, the agency added. Settlers have assaulted farmers, stolen their crops, burnt their land or killed their livestock.
“Families who were once thriving and earning a living from their land are now unable to afford enough food,” Shaun Hughes, WFP country director for Palestine, said in a statement.
“At a time when WFP should be scaling up assistance to reach more people, we are being forced to make difficult decisions, prioritising the most vulnerable while cutting assistance to others despite widespread needs. We urge the international community to act immediately and step up support for Palestinians.”
The funding shortage has also affected WFP operations in Gaza that reach 1.5 million people. In July, the WFP cut the cash value of assistance for 375,000 people by 40 per cent and warned of further cuts if the lack of funding continued.
"Over the next six months from September 2026, WFP urgently requires an additional $386 million to serve an estimated two million food-insecure people across Gaza and the West Bank," the statement said.
Aid operations in Gaza are already suffering under an Israeli blockade, despite a fragile ceasefire that stipulates the free flow of humanitarian assistance into the enclave.
British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said on Tuesday that three UN warehouses were damaged in Gaza's Deir Al Balah during an Israeli strike, while other warehouses operated by the group's partner were extensively damaged in a similar incident in the past week.
Nearly all of Gaza's population of 2.1 million – more than 1.9 million people – need "shelter and essential non-food assistance", the charity added.
Natasha Hall, senior advocate for the Middle East at Refugees International, noted that pressures on the Palestinian economy have increased the need for humanitarian assistance - just as humanitarian funding is shrinking.
She pointed to the loss of work permits in Israel for hundreds of thousands of Palestinians, as well as an increase in settler violence, among the issues fuelling humanitarian need.
"Humanitarian aid has long been a Band-Aid for political and economic issues that could be resolved in quick order should the Israeli government stop putting the squeeze on the PA [Palestinian Authority] and the economy in the West Bank," Ms Hall said.
"Effectively, financially and economically, this area is under siege, and so that reinforces the the need for the WFP and for humanitarian assistance."
The expert, who has lived and worked across the Middle East, also noted that WFP's funding crisis extends far beyond Palestine, impacting other countries including Syria.
items.titleTR: World Food Programme halves number of aid recipients in occupied West Bank

slots.packetSpot:
The World Food Programme announced that, due to insufficient funding, it will reduce the number of people receiving aid in the occupied West Bank from 400,000 to 200,000 in September. According to the agency, food insecurity has more than doubled since 2023; more than 900,000 Palestinians do not have regular access to food, and two-thirds of households have experienced a marked decline in their income.

In Gaza, too, the funding gap is narrowing aid. In July, the World Food Programme reduced the value of cash assistance for 375,000 people by 40 percent; its operations reach 1.5 million people. The agency reported that it urgently needs an additional $386 million in funding to support an estimated two million food-insecure people in Gaza and the West Bank for six months.
slots.packetTitle: Need grows as aid contracts

items.descriptionTR:
Canadian Prime Minister Carney has announced the suspension of Canada-United States trade talks, citing “last-minute changes” made by American negotiators that “were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
Within hours, President Donald Trump’s new Section 338 tariffs, targeting $28 billion in Canadian goods, took effect. Early estimates project that the tariffs could cost 90,000 Canadian jobs.
Until the breakdown in negotiations, the Carney government’s diplomatic posture towards the U.S. had been highly conciliatory. In May, Carney was calling for greater Canada-U.S. integration, arguing that “Canada Strong will help make America great again.”
Now, with trade talks exhausted and fresh economic pain on the way for both Canadians and Americans, conciliation appears to be a spent force. Instead, anger and escalation are taking centre stage.

Read more: Why Mark Carney is pushing ‘Fortress North America’ amid deep Canadian distrust of the U.S.

Asked too much, offered too little
Nobody expected an equal deal between Canada and the U.S. Many of the trade deals struck by the second Trump administration have been deeply one-sided, with the U.S. typically imposing hefty tariffs and extracting commitments from the other party to purchase American goods.
Still, the sheer one-sidedness of the American proposals is galling. Canada would have had to accept hefty tariffs on automobile, steel, aluminium and lumber exports in return for market access it previously enjoyed for decades.
Add to this last-minute demands that would have deeply compromised Canadian sovereignty, including requirements to curtail the protection of the French language — one of the longest running trade policies in Canadian history — and to hold a veto over who Canada can trade with.
For any country, a lopsided deal that penalizes national industries is upsetting. But for Canadians already sensitive to Trump’s taunts and insults, adding last-minute demands to erode sovereignty has been nothing short of enraging.
As Carney put it on Aug. 22:
“We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked … They asked too much and offered too little.”
The new 50 per cent tariff
Up until Aug. 22, most of the Trump administration’s tariffs on Canada followed a basic pattern. Canada was either targeted as part of a broader group of countries — as with the global Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminium — or over a longstanding trade issue, such as softwood lumber.
The 50 per cent tariff breaks with this pattern. As U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has made clear, the point was to force Canada to drop its provincial alcohol bans and lift tariffs on American autos.
In short, Canada is being penalized for defending itself. It’s not clear what’s more troubling: the presumption that America is entitled to sell alcohol to Canadian customers or the belief that it’s illegitimate for Canada to protect its own interests.

Read more: Trump’s new tariffs give Ontario and Québec the perfect excuse to sell their unsold American booze

Retaliation is becoming more palatable
Even before the escalation, 62 per cent of Canadians supported retaliation against U.S. tariff threats. Based on the latest drama, however, that number may climb even higher.
What’s striking about Carney’s response, however, is how quickly and confidently he vowed dollar-for-dollar retaliation. Carney had previously been cool on retaliatory tariffs, even dropping some of Canada’s last September. Now his rapid pivot to retaliation signals not just a change in strategy, but a belief that Canadians — and the country’s global allies — will support it.
Retaliation, however, is not just limited to tariffs. Over the last few days, a war of words has erupted between the Trump administration and Canada’s political leaders, with Ontario Premier Doug Ford saying Trump “can kiss my ass.”
Bloc Québécois leader Yves-François Blanchet is calling for Canada to suspend defence contracts, including the purchase of American F-35 fighter jets. There are options for retaliation that extend far beyond trade.
To say this is unusual for Canadian foreign policy is an understatement. Open threats of retaliation were extremely rare before the Trump administration. And when Canadians did talk about retaliation, there were always fears of being punished by the U.S.
Now, the conversation has flipped and political luminaries like Jean Chrétien, a former Canadian prime minister, are at the front of a very long line calling to “hit where it hurts.”
The U.S. is running out of time
The conventional view is that, in any trade dispute, the U.S. would quickly defeat Canada. The U.S. has a much larger economy, is less reliant on exports to Canada, and, in theory, should more easily absorb any retaliatory measures.
The New York Times has already dismissed Canada’s retaliatory tariffs as having “the effect of a pea shooter in a gun battle.” But this view underestimates Canada’s leverage.
As Nobel-prize winning economist Paul Krugman explains, the U.S. imports economically vital goods from Canada like oil, lumber, electricity and aluminium, for which there is no cheap and accessible domestic substitute. Tariffs on these goods means higher costs for American consumers and businesses in an already inflationary environment.
Foreign governments are acutely aware of these economic problems, and the role they will play in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. As American foreign policy scholar Paul Musgrave argues, this creates incentives for countries to use time as a weapon against the U.S.
For Iran, this could mean keeping oil prices high in order to punish Republicans in the midterms. For Canada, it means leaving Republicans to defend a bitterly unpopular trade war.
It can also mean calibrating tariffs to target areas with vulnerable Republican House and Senate seats, like Ohio, Michigan and Maine. Democratic candidates in these states are already racing to attack Republican incumbents over their support for Trump’s trade war.
The point is not that Canada can defeat the U.S. — it can’t. But it can cause enough pain in the right place, and at the right time, to make a trade war politically costly.
Two views of Canada’s future
In the last 18 months, Canada’s response to the Trump administration has been driven by a specific view of the future.
In this view, the Trump administration may be detestable, but it is only an anomaly and one day it will be gone. When this happens, relations will normalize, so Canada had best not do anything to jeopardize the long-term relationship.
After last weekend, a very different view of the future is emerging. In this view, Canada needed to send a pointed message that the Trump administration had crossed a red line. If the administration does not pay a political price for its aggression, then there will be nothing to deter future administrations from pursuing a similar policy.
Whether Canadians are willing to shoulder the sacrifices required by this sharper view of the future is something only time will tell.
￼
Eric Van Rythoven does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Canada cannot match the U.S. economically, but it can make Donald Trump’s trade war politically costly as the U.S. heads toward midterm elections.
items.titleTR: Mark Carney’s defiance: Canada shows the world how to respond to Donald Trump’s threats

"We would need over half a million 4K TVs to fully display the single Roman image from our largest survey."
NASA's $4.3 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, equipped with a 300-megapixel camera sighted through a refurbished spy mirror, launched Sunday from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on a mission to reveal the mysterious forces driving the Universe.
The new mission will extend the vision of NASA's other famous observatories, providing a field of view 100 times wider than the Hubble Space Telescope and complementing the groundbreaking work of the James Webb Space Telescope. Roman is just the second NASA-led astrophysics mission to launch this century, following the launch of Webb in 2021.
Unlike Webb, which suffered many years of delays before reaching space, Roman arrived at the launch pad nine months before NASA's commitment to send it skyward by May 2027.
Read full article
Comments
items.titleTR: NASA's next "great observatory" begins mission to widen our view of the Universe

slots.packetSpot:
According to NASA, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. The observatory is expected to reach its operational orbit near the Sun-Earth L2 point in about three months; it is planned to be activated and calibrated during the journey, with its first scientific images to be prepared by the end of the year.

Roman is planned to study dark energy, dark matter, galaxies, stars, supernovas and exoplanets through wide-field surveys. NASA says the telescope, which it states has a field of view 100 times that of Hubble, will complement the work of Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope. Designed for a five-year mission, the observatory is named after Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief astronomer and one of the advocates of space-based telescopes.
slots.packetTitle: A wider window on the universe

Naomi Osaka advanced to the second round of the US Open in New York after defeating Russia’s Anastasia Zakharova 7-6 (8-6), 7-6 (7-3) in the first round. Osaka arrived on court before the match in a white hooded outfit featuring newspaper-headline clippings about key moments in her career, wearing a black basketball-style jersey underneath.

Osaka said her on-court look was inspired by retired NBA star Allen Iverson. She said she sees Iverson as a pioneer in fashion and admires him for his influence on the way athletes express themselves through clothing.

Osaka, a former world No. 1 with four Grand Slam titles and the tournament’s 13th seed, won the US Open in 2018 and 2020. Osaka, who will face Czech player Katerina Siniakova in the second round, also said she wanted to show more outfits.

As national mourning was declared, the flag at the palace was lowered to half-mast; those gathered outside the Royal Palace in Oslo left flowers and flags.

Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the entire country was mourning. European monarchs, world leaders and representatives of international institutions also issued messages of condolence.

At least four Palestinians, including two children and one woman, were killed in Israeli airstrikes carried out during the operation, according to health officials. Heavy bombardment, gunfire and struck vehicles were reported in the Katiba area of western Gaza. Hamas and the Hamas-run media office in Gaza argued that the special forces operation had been exposed, describing it as a ceasefire violation and a serious crime; the Hamas-run media office also alleged that some special forces personnel had been killed. The Israeli military, meanwhile, said none of its soldiers had been wounded.

Accounts conflict over whether Israeli-backed anti-Hamas Palestinian militias were also present in the area: Palestinian media wrote that these groups had entered the area, while some Israeli outlets alleged that only a local armed militia was operating on the ground.

items.descriptionTR:
FTC says firm replaces actual ad-auction results "with higher prices set by Amazon."
The Federal Trade Commission and 22 states sued Amazon yesterday, alleging that it has conducted a secret scheme to overcharge advertisers for seven years.
"Since 2019, Amazon.com, Inc. has secretly and systematically overcharged its approximately 1.2 million advertising customers by manipulating the 'auctions' that it uses to set the price of ads on its platform," the lawsuit said. "Amazon represents, and advertisers believe, that competitive auctions set the prices for advertising on its leading e-commerce website. But, in reality, Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits."
The FTC said it obtained internal documents and messages that reveal how Amazon secretly inflated auction prices for Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, and Sponsored Display advertisements that appear alongside results seen by consumers when they search for a product. The FTC investigation began in 2024.
Read full article
Comments
items.titleTR: FTC alleges Amazon illegally made $20 billion by rigging billions of ad auctions

slots.packetSpot:
The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the attorneys general of 22 states have filed a lawsuit against Amazon in the US District Court for the Western District of Washington. The lawsuit alleges that the company has secretly altered its advertising auctions since 2019, charging roughly 1.2 million advertising customers higher fees and potentially collecting more than $20 billion through undisclosed “soft reserve” surcharges.

In its claim based on internal correspondence and documents, the FTC argues that Amazon replaced the system it presented as a competitive second-price auction with prices set by the company itself. Regulators are seeking to halt the practice, as well as fines, compensation and other financial penalties.

Amazon describes the lawsuit as “misguided.” The company, which acknowledges using reserve prices, says advertisers never pay more than their bids under any circumstances; it says the system reflects the relevance of the advertisement and the market value of advertising space. Amazon also states that the inflation-adjusted average cost per click remained flat between 2019 and 2024, and that relevance-based selection saved advertisers more than $8 billion over the 2021-2025 period.
slots.packetTitle: Amazon’s ad auctions face court challenge

items.descriptionTR:
The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics
Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.
In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”.
Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of his position on military spending.
Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation.
Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.”
Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.”
items.titleTR: Burnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PM

slots.packetSpot:
Andy Burnham’s first speech in the House of Commons as UK prime minister highlights the political narrative through which he is setting his government’s direction. According to The Guardian, Burnham criticised the past decade through the “wrong turns” he linked to Brexit and choices made during Margaret Thatcher’s era; he said the next decade could be better, promising growth, optimism and to put local needs before party.

Burnham, who took office more than six weeks ago, also stressed that he wanted to work with opposition parties. Housing, devolution, Northern Ireland, Europe, the climate, political donations, online abuse, settlements in the West Bank and energy were discussed during the session, which lasted more than three hours. No new surprise policy announcements were made; it was stated that final decisions had not yet been made on some issues.
slots.packetTitle: Burnham charts a new course in the Commons

According to prosecutors, Santiago recorded the attack’s livestream and published the manifesto of the two teenage attackers; she faces three murder charges and one conspiracy charge for aiding and abetting the crime.

To pour a little more salt into the wound, Boyd hasn’t fared well against the Brewers throughout his career, as he has a 9.00 ERA in five starts, allowing nine home runs, 16 walks, and 30 hits.
With the offense looking like it’s going to be the name of the game tonight, the Brewers will continue to go with the home run-heavy top of the lineup. As will the Cubs tonight, as they’re fresh off of the second most home runs hit by an MLB team in history with nine last night. The man who had three of them last night, Alex Bregman, will be in the three spot of their lineup last night.
As the calendar flips to September, reinforcements enter the clubhouse. Earlier this afternoon, the Brewers recalled Bo Naylor from Triple-A Nashville, giving the team their third catcher on the active roster. The second reinforcement comes in the left-hander JoJo Romero, who will look to make his Brewers debut tonight. Before the trade with the Cardinals, Romero had appeared in 44 games, recording 20 holds while posting a 3.51 ERA.
