items.descriptionTR:
Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s ordeal, but never fully reckons with what her notoriety meant for breaking
Early in Netflix’s new documentary, Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly, Australian B-girl Rachael Gunn, recounts a session she had with her sports psychologist prior to the 2024 Paris Olympics.
“Right before the Olympics, I went to my therapist, panicked,” she says. Her therapist asked her what was the worst thing that could happen. And she said, “The whole world could laugh at me.” Her therapist responded: “Do you think that’s reasonable?” Cue Gunn’s hysterical laughter.
items.titleTR: The Raygun documentary ducks a big question about the Olympic fame of a ‘dorky white academic’

slots.packetSpot:
Netflix’s Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly documentary retells with warmth and humour the global ridicule Australian B-girl Rachael Gunn faced after her performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics. The film focuses on her personal story through interviews with Gunn’s family, husband and dancers from Australia’s breaking community.

Gunn received no votes from any of the nine judges across her six rounds in Paris; nevertheless, her performance quickly became the subject of memes, late-night shows, conspiracy theories and a musical at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival. The documentary addresses claims that she entered the Olympics through cheating, which are false.

According to the criticism, the documentary does not sufficiently examine the broader significance for breaking of Gunn becoming the world’s most recognisable breaker overnight. Breaking will not be included in the programme for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics; it is stated that this decision was unrelated to Gunn and was made months before Paris. The World DanceSport Federation has submitted breaking for consideration for the 2032 Olympics, which Brisbane will host.
slots.packetTitle: Breaking in Raygun’s shadow

items.descriptionTR:
Colin Kaepernick still watches football. The former San Francisco 49ers quarterback told NBC News in an interview that he prefers to watch the college game instead. The 38-year-old Kaepernick, who led the 49ers to a Super Bowl after the 2012 season, hasn't played since the 2016 season finale, an exile that began not long after he started taking a knee during the national anthem to highlight social injustices.
NEW YORK (AP) — Colin Kaepernick still watches football.
Just not the NFL.
The former San Francisco 49ers quarterback told NBC News in an interview that he prefers to watch the college game instead.
The 38-year-old Kaepernick, who led the 49ers to a Super Bowl after the 2012 season, hasn't played since the 2016 season finale, an exile that began not long after he started taking a knee during the national anthem to highlight social injustices.
“I’m not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well,” Kaepernick said.
Kaepernick and former teammate Eric Reid, who knelt alongside Kaepernick, sued the NFL citing collusion. The two sides settled in early 2019.
During a hiatus that eventually became a retirement, Kaepernick has stayed busy. His “Know Your Rights” camps are designed to educate young people and his foundation helps pay for independent autopsies, including recently for Mississippi teenager Nolan Wells.
Asked by the network if he thinks about his legacy at all, Kaepernick said it doesn't cross his mind.
“What I think about is what are the areas that I can do work that I think are going to have an impact and help us move towards that future together," he said. "At the end of the day, people will decide what that legacy is, and hopefully that’s a positive one.”
___
See AP’s full NFL coverage here
items.titleTR: Report: Kaepernick says that a decade after taking a knee, he shuns the NFL for 'blackballing' him

slots.packetSpot:
Colin Kaepernick says that, a decade after the protest he began during the national anthem while wearing a San Francisco 49ers jersey in 2016, he no longer watches or supports the NFL. He attributes this to his claim that the league excluded him and targeted other players who joined the protest; he says he watches college football.

Kaepernick did not play in the NFL again after opting out of his contract in 2017 and filed a grievance alleging that team owners had conspired to keep him out of the league. The grievances filed by Kaepernick and his former teammate Eric Reid were settled by the NFL in 2019.

The NFL launched the Inspire Change programme in 2019; in 2020, Commissioner Roger Goodell condemned racism and systemic oppression of Black people, saying the league had been wrong not to listen to NFL players earlier. Kaepernick, however, considers these steps performative and argues that the league has not changed in any substantive way.
slots.packetTitle: Kaepernick's unfinished reckoning with the NFL

items.descriptionTR: The 21-year-old Belgium international joins on a five-year contract to become Newcastle's eighth new arrival of a busy summer.
items.titleTR: Newcastle sign Matias Fernandez-Pardo in €60m transfer from Lille

slots.packetSpot:
Newcastle United have completed the signing of Belgian forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille. According to The Athletic, the 21-year-old has joined on a five-year contract for €60 million plus bonuses.

Fernandez-Pardo scored eight goals last season, starting 27 of Lille's 34 Ligue 1 matches; Lille finished third in the league to qualify for the Champions League. Able to play on the left wing or at centre-forward, he will wear the number 20 shirt and could make his debut against Bournemouth on Saturday.
slots.packetTitle: Newcastle's new attacking face

items.descriptionTR: Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay is to have a minor heart procedure after the discovery of "a mild benign arrhythmia", Napoli have announced.
items.titleTR: McTominay to miss Scotland games with minor heart issue

slots.packetSpot:
According to Napoli's statement, Scott McTominay has developed a mild and benign heart rhythm disorder. The 29-year-old midfielder will undergo a corrective procedure using cardiac arrhythmia ablation (PFA) in the coming days; the club said he will be ready again after the international break.

McTominay is expected to miss Napoli's next four matches: the away trip to Inter, the Arsenal match, and fixtures against Bologna and Fiorentina. He is also not expected to play in Scotland's Nations League matches against Slovenia, Switzerland and North Macedonia.
slots.packetTitle: A pause in McTominay's rhythm

items.descriptionTR: The 22-year-old midfielder has agreed terms on a six-year contract with the option of a further 12 months
items.titleTR: Chelsea agree £47m Lamine Camara transfer with Monaco

slots.packetSpot:
According to The Athletic, Chelsea have had an improved offer of around £47 million (€54 million) for Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara accepted. An earlier €45 million offer is reported to have been rejected.

According to the report, 22-year-old Camara agreed terms on a six-year contract with an option for a 12-month extension; he completed his medical and was expected to arrive in London. The move came after Chelsea agreed to sell Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City for £125 million.
slots.packetTitle: Chelsea close in on Camara midfield move

items.descriptionTR: Frenchwoman Lois Boisson has provided the first big blow-up of the US Open, smashing her racquet in disgust after going down in three sets to American 26th seed Emma Navarro.
items.titleTR: French young gun has racquet-smashing meltdown, defending champs advance

slots.packetSpot:
Emma Navarro and Loïs Boisson’s rain-interrupted US Open first-round match in New York was completed the following day. Navarro reportedly won the contest 7-6(6), 6-7(1), 6-3.

The match ended after Boisson lost three consecutive points following the break point she earned in the final game. The racket-breaking incident after the match stood out as the dramatic image of the result.
slots.packetTitle: The image left after a match

items.descriptionTR: Stefanos Tsitsipas says he was not surprised when it was revealed that Nick Kyrgios had been suspended after testing positive to cocaine.
items.titleTR: Former rival says Nick Kyrgios's drug ban 'pretty much expected'

slots.packetSpot:
Stefanos Tsitsipas said he had been aware of Nick Kyrgios’s positive cocaine test before the public announcement and that the provisional suspension did not surprise him. Tsitsipas stated that he had heard allegations from people on the tour regarding Kyrgios’s off-court behaviour, and therefore expected disciplinary action to come sooner.

According to the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA), the cocaine metabolite benzoylecgonine was detected in a sample Kyrgios provided at the Mallorca Championships on 22 June; the finding was confirmed on 17 July by a World Anti-Doping Agency-accredited laboratory. The mandatory provisional suspension imposed by the ITIA on 4 August was announced on 19 August. Kyrgios accepted the positive test and apologised; he had not exercised his right to appeal when the decision was announced. During the suspension, he will not be able to play, coach or participate in events sanctioned by professional tennis bodies, Grand Slams and national federations.
slots.packetTitle: The expected suspension

items.descriptionTR:
Comments signal president prepared to use dispute to push UK to raise defence spending and Nato contributions
Donald Trump has suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, in a move likely to strain the “special relationship” between Washington and London.
“I always review every position – that’s just one of many,” the US president told reporters in the White House, in response to a question about whether he was reviewing the US’s position over the South Atlantic islands, an archipelago whose status has long been disputed by Argentina, which claims sovereignty.
items.titleTR: Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland Islands

slots.packetSpot:
Donald Trump, when asked at the White House whether the US position on sovereignty over the Falkland Islands was being reviewed, said he evaluates every position; he did not promise a policy change. While the US officially maintains neutrality on sovereignty, it recognises British administration; Argentina claims sovereignty over the islands.

It had previously been reported that an unnamed US official said Washington could change its position if Britain failed to meet its defence-spending commitments. It is suggested that the issue could be used to pressure London over defence spending and NATO contributions. The British government, meanwhile, stresses that the islanders are British and have the right to determine their future.
slots.packetTitle: A signal of review over the Falklands

items.descriptionTR: Thailand's coastal city of Pattaya is preparing for a visit by the USS Abraham Lincoln, as the aircraft carrier makes its way back to the U.S. following a grueling deployment in the Middle East
items.titleTR: Thailand's Pattaya anticipates USS Abraham Lincoln visit

items.descriptionTR:
Security stepped up in Pattaya before arrival of thousands of sailors and marines whose deployment was extended due to US war in Iran
Authorities in the Thai resort city of Pattaya have stepped up security as they prepare to welcome thousands of sailors and marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln who have spent more than 270 consecutive days at sea.
“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” the provincial governor, Narit Niramaiwong, told AFP.
items.titleTR: Thai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at sea

slots.packetSpot:
Security and transport preparations have accelerated in Pattaya ahead of USS Abraham Lincoln’s port visit on its way back to the United States. Thai officials expect a significant portion of the more than 5,000 US personnel aboard the ship to come into the city; the police presence is being increased, while businesses are being warned against excessive pricing.

Accounts differ over whether the ship’s uninterrupted time at sea during its lengthy Middle East deployment exceeded 250 days or 270 days. Reports concerning living conditions, mental health and supply shortages had emerged during the deployment. Lincoln is expected to return to the United States after its port call in Thailand.

The local administration hopes the visit will create a boost for tourism and the economy. However, some business operators are not sure how many of those expected to arrive, even though thousands are said to be coming, will spend money in Pattaya.
slots.packetTitle: A shore break in Pattaya

items.descriptionTR:
British far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’
Milo Yiannopoulos, the British far-right commentator who was arrested last week by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Louisiana and deported to the United Kingdom, has broken his silence about the experience, saying that “for the first time I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified”.
Yiannopoulos on Tuesday appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored, a YouTube show presented by Piers Morgan, the British broadcaster and media personality. Yiannopoulos, 41, described the experience in the US as “humiliating and disorientating”, “physically degrading” and “frightening”.
items.titleTR: Deported Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ‘ashamed’ of support for Trump

slots.packetSpot:
Milo Yiannopoulos’s deportation from the United States brought together his account of the detention process and his regret over having supported Trump. ICE reportedly detained him at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Louisiana, and the Department of Homeland Security reportedly deported him to the United Kingdom the following day.

According to federal authorities, Yiannopoulos entered the United States legally on 14 May; a final deportation order was issued against him on 22 July because he failed to attend an immigration hearing. Yiannopoulos, however, said he had not overstayed his visa, that he held an O-1 visa and had applied to convert his status to a green card; he argued that hearing notices had been sent to his old address.

Speaking on Piers Morgan’s YouTube programme, Yiannopoulos described what he experienced as humiliating, disorienting and frightening; he claimed to have seen “cruelty” in the process. Claiming that the Trump administration had become one under Laura Loomer’s influence, he said he was “very ashamed” of having supported Trump. Loomer had claimed credit for reporting Yiannopoulos to ICE.
slots.packetTitle: Regret after deportation

items.descriptionTR: GoPro is merging with a company that builds AI infrastructure, and will continue supporting existing consumer products.
items.titleTR: GoPro to be acquired for $285M, will remain a public company

slots.packetSpot: Starman Optical has reportedly agreed to acquire GoPro in a $285 million merger. The transaction, expected to be completed by the end of the year, highlights the company’s plan to move into areas connected to optics, defense and AI infrastructure while continuing its consumer products.
slots.packetTitle: GoPro turns toward optics and AI infrastructure

items.descriptionTR: AMSTERDAM, Sept 1 - Dutch police on Tuesday said 34 suspects from several countries were arrested after a shooting in which a man was killed and two police officers were wounded in the early hours.
items.titleTR: Dutch police arrest 34 people after shooting in rural village

slots.packetSpot:
Thirty-four suspects were detained after a shooting in the Dutch village of Overasselt in which one person was killed and two police officers were injured. The injured officers are reportedly recovering in hospital, but no details about their injuries were shared.

The incident reportedly occurred in the early morning, about 135 kilometres southeast of Amsterdam. Residents were asked to remain in their homes while the investigation continues. Security camera footage shows about 30 people, most wearing ski masks and carrying weapons, walking along a street and fleeing after the apparent shooting; police are examining the footage.

It was announced that those detained include people from the Netherlands, France, Belgium and Algeria. Details about their identities and possible charges have not yet been announced. While authorities described the violence as extreme and unprecedented, prosecutors and police did not comment on a possible motive; the incident is said to appear to have been a gang-related attack.
slots.packetTitle: Overasselt under the shadow of violence

items.descriptionTR:
Early Saturday afternoon at the Daisy Chain Fields festival, in Irvine, California, the 25-year-old singer Eli twirled in a tank top emblazoned with a cartoon guitar while singing songs whose plasticky violins recalled the kind of music played on the Disney Channel in 2004. Dancers waved poles with dresses attached to them as if they were flags. She took out her phone, whose case was shaped like a cute bear, and read some thoughts she’d jotted down.
“This journal entry is to show you my fundamental belief that we must redistribute wealth,” she said. “We must love our neighbors no matter what they believe or don’t. We must unite with each other and radicalize. Eat the identity politics that deceive and divide us all, as well as”—here she broke into a ragged moan—“eating the rich!”
Eli is a campy artist of questionable earnestness, but her statement was in line with the mood of Daisy Chain—a place where girlish aesthetics that are so often seen as frivolous could accompany calls for revolution. Organized by the 23-year-old pop star Olivia Rodrigo, the inaugural edition of the festival featured an all-female lineup and raised $20 million—half of which was donated by Melinda French Gates—for an array of women’s-rights organizations, including Planned Parenthood and the National Domestic Workers Alliance. Even as a brutal heat wave threatened to smother the energy, the fest felt like a cheerful coming-out party—an announcement of the political commitments of a generation of mainstream artists more famous for singing about the self than about society.  
Rodrigo patterned Daisy Chain off of Lilith Fair, the best-selling female-fronted touring festival that ran from 1997 to 1999, but the two events are a study in contrasts. Lilith’s co-founder Sarah McLachlan wanted to prove the viability of female musicians at a time when, she told the LA Times, radio programmers were reluctant to play two of them back-to-back. The lineup reflected a boom in singer-songwriters—Tracy Chapman, Jewel, Paula Cole, Indigo Girls—whose socially conscientious songs harkened back to the spirit of Woodstock (an obvious influence on the flower-powery Daisy Chain as well). Lilith’s aesthetics were earthen and earnest—a celebration of an ideal of strong, serious womanhood, much to the perturbation of late-night comics who cracked jokes about Cole’s armpit hair.
Today, women aren’t so marginal to the record industry; in fact, it can sometimes seem like Taylor Swift and her disciples are the record industry. But with power has come an inversion in content and style. The dominant female musical archetype of the 2020s isn’t the diva or the chanteuse—it’s the girlie, a term that conveys knowing immaturity and kitsch femininity. Girlies write songs about kinky sex while calling themselves princesses (as does the Daisy Chain singer Chappell Roan), or rap tough and fast while slathered in Barbie-pink body paint (as Doechii did on Saturday). The word is gendered, but it refers to a disposition, and thus can encompass gay guys and even those shy and sweet straight men known as babygirls.
Daisy Chain was for the girlies. Irvine’s Great Park was turned into a Lewis Carroll wonderland pocked with floral arrangements that seemed like crayon drawings come to life. Young kids ran around in tiaras while adults blended frilliness and adolescent-alternative stylings: blond locks with streaks of slime green, or the undying rebel-girl look of baby-doll dresses and Doc Martens. I wondered whether the commitment to daintiness explained even the dearth of shade at the fest; the tasseled umbrellas dotting the grounds were totally adorable and terribly unmatched to an El Niño August.
Girlie nation has arisen slowly, over decades. As my colleague Sophie Gilbert reported in her book Girl on Girl, Lilith Fair’s vision of female artistry was sidelined as record labels and radio stations began to favor smiling, pliable teenagers such as Britney Spears. Twenty-first-century youths grew up with former Mouseketeers serving as aspirational figures—and, eventually, as cautionary tales about giving up one’s agency for fame. Following in the example of Swift, who built on her teen-princess image with her own formidable songwriting, the new female guard arose. Some, like Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter, were trained by Disney; others, like Billie Eilish and Rachel Chinouriri (an ascendant U.K. singer and a Daisy Chain booking), got their start at home, posting music online. All of them project control with every slickly witty, emotionally frank, personally revealing hit they write.
What they haven’t projected much of, in their songs, at least, is the political edge of the Lilith crowd. Jewel broke out with an album whose title song made a shockingly frontal attack on bigotry (“You say he’s a faggot; does he make you sick to your stomach?”). But today’s young stars mostly just side-eye society’s problems in lyrical tales of hookups, breakups, and anxiety. When Roan calls for a “Femininomenon” (one song title), she’s implicitly calling for feminist change, but she’s explicitly calling just for more girls to ditch their dudes.
It’s not that Gen Z has nothing to say—many of these singers will readily riff about ICE and Gaza on their Instagram and in public comments. Rodrigo even delivered an onstage F.U. to the Supreme Court after the fall of national abortion rights, in 2022. But when it comes to their music, they prefer to focus mostly on the personal. Perhaps that’s because their milieu is the isolation and intimacy of the smartphone-enabled bedroom, not the social jungle of rock clubs and coffee shops. Maybe it’s because they watched progressive pop of the mid-2010s cheer Hillary Clinton’s failed presidential campaign and then spin itself into an even more didactic fervor during Donald Trump’s first term. On some level, girliehood may be a defensive posture amid conservative cultural backlash: a way to speak and shout and command lots of influence without being seen as threatening.
Indeed, Daisy Chain inevitably raised the question of how potent mere cultural visibility can be. Lines of people snaked through the grounds throughout the day—some for art installations by female artists, and many for immersive brand activations, including a pink, larger-than-life Taco Bell Baja Blast that had been scrawled on with diary-cursive font. The festival was a co-production of the convicted monopoly Live Nation and felt, in execution, like a re-skinned version of moneymaking glitz fests such as Coachella. Eli’s rallying cry with a side of giggles aside, the fest was not destabilizing power structures—it was part of them. Rodrigo is probably not the person to figure out what true counterculture might mean in this, the most consumerist decade of human history.
Still, she’s trying. Daisy Chain’s two stages were festooned with mock buttons, like on a backpack, that advertised the fest’s 10 nonprofit beneficiaries (representatives for which got to speak to the crowds before various sets). This great design decision served whimsical eye candy, evoked a lineage of hippies and women’s libbers, and dispensed useful information. The featured slogans—Bans off our bodies, Reproductive rights are human rights, WOMEN ROCK BETTER—hardly read like safe platitudes in post-Dobbs America, where some conservatives now openly yearn to roll back women’s right to vote.
Rodrigo is also at last tackling overt protest music. Shortly before the festival, she released a coolly seething post-punk single called “Serena Joy,” named for a character in The Handmaid’s Tale. Its exact concerns are a bit hazy: A lyric about gold-painted towers indirectly sneers at Trump, and a mention of bothered “neighbors” could be about ICE deportations or even tariffs on Canada. What’s clear is her overall call to wake up and fight back. I get shivers when she sings, “If you can’t throw a punch / You can learn how to spit.”
The fest’s lineup also made a statement by tracing an intergenerational feminist lineage instead of just spotlighting trendy new acts. One invitee was the ’90s rock band Garbage, whose singer, Shirley Manson, made painfully heartfelt speeches about resilience, growing older, and LGBTQ acceptance. Another was the indie band the Breeders, whose cooed harmonies and twisted guitars are the bay-leaf influence on Rodrigo’s tangiest songs. The reggae-inflected alternative singer Santigold—a representative of the 2000s indie landscape—invited members of the crowd onstage for a joyful, if less than impressively skilled, dance contest.
The most telling booking was Bikini Kill, the punk band whose riot-grrrl sound flipped clichés about demure young womanhood way back in the early ’90s. The lead singer, Kathleen Hanna, opened with some political scene setting: “This government hates us and wants us dead. They don’t give a shit about anybody’s health care. They don’t care if we’re dying in parking lots of curable illnesses.” Then she got to croaking and gyrating with a ferocity that offered a reminder to the Instagram-generation viewers that playing pretty isn’t the only way to command eyeballs. “This is the most engaged crowd I’ve ever seen in my life,” she said at one point, and a reason was clear: At Bikini Kill’s early shows, she would call for men to make room for girls to come to the front of the crowd, but here, she didn’t need to do that.
[Read: How indie rock changed the world]
Still, the festival’s greatest highlights came from gutsy and well-executed performances by young people. The first act of the day, the experimental electronic-pop artist Quiet Light, offered a calm and cooling welcome as she executed slow choreo in a billowing nightie. Later, the blue-haired songwriter Devon Again—a last-minute replacement after the girl group Katseye dropped out—knocked me back with country-tinged electro rock as crunchy as a kettle chip. In a stunt that recalled bros such as Blink-182 and Red Hot Chili Peppers, her band members dropped trou at the start of the set and rocked in their boxers.
As the sun fell, Roan took to the stage for a happy-go-lucky display of dominance. Her band, dressed in snazzy ’80s power suits, whipped up simmering disco tension punctuated by Van Halen–style guitar eruptions. Roan, who was styled like a flight attendant from the ’90s sci-fi movie The Fifth Element, also acted all-business: spare with her banter and springy on her feet as she flicked between chatty verses and lung-busting choruses.
After that stratospheric spectacle, Rodrigo’s headlining set felt a bit like a wobbly-legged return to Earth. Although she can dig deep and nail the big moments—“The Cure” sounded bottomlessly sad—she often leans too heavily on actorly tics that overplay the considerable personality already inherent in her lyrics. Listening to her sing her stellar recent song “Maggots for Brains,” I had the thought that her songwriting talent, bar for bar, matches almost any of her predecessors’. Just then, some predecessors joined her: first McLachlan, for a festival-shushing rendition of “Building a Mystery” and “Angel,” and then Alanis Morissette, to grin and yowl “Ironic.” The Gen X parents in the crowd, clearly worn down by a day of sticky-hot chaperoning, suddenly came alive.
The final song of the night was the most moving one: Rodrigo and Stevie Nicks, another special guest, singing “Landslide.” Their delivery was so careful and crystalline that no one could miss the relevance of the lyrics about generations bound together by time’s forward march. When Nicks sang, “Yes, I’m getting older too,” on her own, with a sad smile, my gut twisted at the thought of the trailblazers we’ve lost lately. But Nicks also conveyed hope—because today’s girls are only at the beginning of what they’ll accomplish.
Cutesy aesthetics met calls for revolution at Olivia Rodrigo’s new music festival.
items.titleTR: Woodstock, Lilith Fair, and Taco Bell Rolled Into One

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Tens of thousands of music lovers descended on Great Park in Irvine, Calif., over the weekend to scream along to their favourite artists — part of a history-making event to raise funds for women's health, reproductive rights and ending gender-based violence.
items.titleTR: Olivia Rodrigo's music festival raises $20M US for charities that help women and girls

slots.packetSpot:
Olivia Rodrigo’s inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival, held at Great Park in Irvine, California, brought together a female-led lineup and a programme focused on women’s rights, pairing new-generation pop stars with older-generation names such as Bikini Kill, Garbage and the Breeders. The $10 million announced before the festival reached $20 million with a matching $10 million from Melinda French Gates; proceeds were directed to Planned Parenthood, the National Institute for Reproductive Health, Black Mamas Matter Alliance, the National Domestic Workers Alliance and other nonprofit partners.

Women’s health, reproductive rights and work against gender-based violence were also prominent through art installations, activist content and representatives of organisations at the festival site. At the event, inspired by Lilith Fair founded by Sarah McLachlan, McLachlan, Alanis Morissette and Stevie Nicks joined Rodrigo on stage.

The event coincided with a period in which struggles over reproductive rights in the United States intensified following the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. While the festival’s political visibility was emphasised, its co-production with Live Nation and comparisons with large commercial festivals such as Coachella also raised the question of the place of that visibility within a commercial structure.
slots.packetTitle: Pop’s stage for women’s rights

items.descriptionTR:
When the Amish man emerged from his barn to greet me, he had no idea that his newborn son’s death had become national news. The man wore a straw hat, black trousers, and suspenders over a long-sleeved blue shirt; one of his similarly dressed sons was guiding a horse-drawn plow in a nearby field.

The man told me that, like most Amish people, he and his family don’t watch TV or use the internet. They don’t read the newspaper either. So they didn’t know until I told them that last Tuesday, Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, held a press conference to announce the first two “measles-associated” deaths in the state in 35 years. Both of the people who died were from Lancaster County, which is home to the largest Amish community in the country and has been hardest hit by the state’s months-long measles outbreak.

They also didn’t know that Shapiro’s political opponents are accusing him of using the deaths to score political points, or that the county’s coroner later told reporters that his office had performed an autopsy on an infant who tested positive for measles but that the cause of death had been a ruptured spleen. The confusion led Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the secretary of health and human services, to mock Shapiro on X, calling his press conference “unseemly” and an example of “the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain.” Without evidence, Kennedy wrote that “the deaths may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers.”

The Amish man asked me not to reveal his and his family’s names or exactly where they live, to protect the family’s privacy. His son has not been publicly identified as the newborn whose death has been the subject of so much controversy. But the circumstances of the death match, and when I told him about the case that had made the news, he said it sounded like his son. When I ran the family’s biographical details past the Lancaster County coroner, Stephen Diamantoni, he said that the office was not currently investigating any additional infant deaths in the area. When further pressed, Diamantoni said he could neither confirm nor deny the identity of the child whose death his office was investigating.

The story the baby’s father told me filled in many details missing from the accounts of both the coroner and the state. And it made clear that, amid the political squabble and competing theories, an actual family is grieving the death of their child.


I spent part of yesterday afternoon speaking with the newborn’s father and mother, whom I’ll call John and Anna. After John and I had been talking for a while, Anna came out of the house, and—although hesitant at first—agreed to join us. We sat at a table on their porch, which overlooks their postcard-beautiful farm, tucked away down a long gravel driveway. They mostly grow corn on their 45 acres, along with some hay and tobacco. They have a well-tended garden next to the house, and a small chicken coop. They’ve lived on the property for 20 years and have 13 children, some of whom stood nearby on the porch to listen or peered out through one of the screen-covered windows.

About a month ago, John and Anna became aware that measles was spreading in their community. At last count, Lancaster County has recorded 210 cases so far this year. Besides John, no one in the family had been vaccinated against the virus. John told me he’d heard from someone that this strain of measles wasn’t dangerous for pregnant women, but he wasn’t sure whether to believe it. (In fact, measles, regardless of the strain, can cause serious pregnancy complications.) Anna, who was pregnant, worried about the effect measles might have on her baby, but she didn’t think she could avoid being exposed. “I saw we can’t even get away from it because so many people have it,” she told me. Even if Anna had wanted to get vaccinated then, it would have been too late: The CDC recommends against giving the vaccine to pregnant women.

Sure enough, a few weeks ago, one of John and Anna’s older children got sick. The rest of them soon followed. Two of the children became dehydrated and required IVs. Anna became extremely ill, at one point spiking a fever of 102 degrees. She struggled to hold down food and fluids. For days, she could speak only in a whisper. On August 13, she was taken to a clinic to get an IV for dehydration.

The next day, she went into labor. Anna remembers being very weak. “I didn’t have a single piece of energy,” she told me. The baby was delivered at a birthing center by the same midwife who had attended the births of Anna’s other children and, remarkably, Anna’s own birth. The baby, who weighed seven pounds, was born a little after 5 p.m. on August 14. They knew right away that something was wrong: He had a pulse, but he wasn’t breathing. The midwife contacted paramedics, who arrived within minutes. John recalled them giving the newborn oxygen and gentle chest compressions with two thumbs, to no avail. It was all over in less than half an hour. The paramedics told them that the county coroner would need to be contacted to take the body.

As John and Anna spoke with me, one of their sons, who recently turned 1, played with a toy horse and buggy while one of their daughters bounced an orange ball against the table. Anna and John were somber but matter-of-fact about their son’s death. “There’s nothing we can do about it,” Anna told me. John said he viewed the tragedy as part of God’s plan, and pointed out that other parents lose children too. “I guess he chose us this time,” he told me.


Neither John nor Anna has strong feelings about vaccination. Anna told me she wasn’t sure why her parents didn’t get her any shots. Choosing not to immunize their children wasn’t a political statement, and they didn’t make the decision after extensive research. They just didn’t do it.

Pennsylvania allows children to attend school without being vaccinated if their parents object on religious or moral grounds. Though the Amish Church has no official doctrine against vaccines, the vaccination rate among the Amish tends to be low: Last year, the state’s health department estimated that only 25 percent of the Amish community in Lancaster County had received the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. In 2021, Kennedy declared that the United States needs to “think more like the Amish” at an Amish country fair just a short drive from where John and Anna live. Standing under a big white tent, Kennedy also joked about measles, saying that when he and his siblings caught the disease, they had to “stay at home and watch TV the whole week.” That got a big laugh. He also said the best treatment for measles is vitamin A and chicken soup—a statement that Shapiro has been using to attack Kennedy’s vaccine beliefs since he announced the two measles-associated deaths in his state.

Because they don’t follow the news, John and Anna weren’t aware of the controversy between Shapiro and Kennedy. In fact, they didn’t know who either man was. John said that he had recently received a voicemail from someone saying that a man named Kennedy wanted to speak with him, but he didn’t return the call. (An HHS spokesperson declined to answer questions about that call, instead criticizing Shapiro for prematurely speaking about the measles-associated deaths.) John’s father told them that the local newspaper had published a story about a baby who had died, and that it sounded as though the baby could be theirs, but they weren’t sure. They also didn’t think that their baby’s death was much of a mystery. They assumed that Anna’s severe case of measles contributed to their loss. That’s what the midwife told them as well.

Arguments over whether measles caused the infant’s death have largely centered around the lacerated spleen. It’s a confusing detail. When children acquire measles, the infection can lead to an enlarged spleen, which is more likely to burst. To some people, that might seem like clear evidence that the infant died because of measles. But Diamantoni, the coroner, has publicly maintained that his office believes that the spleen was not enlarged and therefore that the cause of death was not related to measles. (Prominent physicians have since pointed out that a ruptured spleen may not look enlarged even if it was affected by measles.) “I’ve had several discussions with our forensic pathologist, and he feels adamantly that this was not a measles death and that it was a traumatic rupture of his spleen,” Diamantoni told me. He also noted that the investigation was still ongoing and he wasn’t sure when it would be completed.

Diamantoni told me he is “very in favor of immunization,” but questioning whether measles really contributed to measles-associated deaths is becoming more typical among anti-vaccine activists. Last year, two young girls died in West Texas’s massive measles outbreak. Not long after their funerals, anti-vaccine activists reframed their deaths as caused by something other than the measles. Yes, they had the measles, the argument went, but really they died from another infection or hospital error. Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization Kennedy founded before becoming HHS secretary, aggressively pushed that narrative.

What anti-vaccine activists usually neglect to mention is that measles, which can temporarily hamper the immune system’s memory, sets the stage for other infections. Most young children who die from measles are actually killed by pneumonia after their immune system has been overwhelmed. But they almost certainly wouldn’t have died if not for measles.


What exactly happened to John and Anna’s son remains unclear. A ruptured spleen is extremely rare in newborns in any circumstance, and so far the coroner hasn’t determined what could have caused it. John and Anna told me they had no idea either. In fact, they hadn’t heard anything about a ruptured spleen until I mentioned the coroner’s public comments to them; they simply knew that Anna had been sick, and then they had lost their child. John told me he had called the coroner’s office on Friday but was told that the investigation was still under way. They were surprised that details of their baby’s case were being discussed—if indeed the case that has captured national attention is their son’s—while they were still waiting to hear from the coroner and eager to read his report once the investigation had concluded. When I asked Diamantoni why he hadn’t been in touch with John and Anna, he said, speaking generally, that “there may be lots of factors that go into when a notification is made,” but didn’t elaborate further.

John and Anna’s son’s body was returned to them on August 17. He is buried in a cemetery a few miles away from their home. A small mound of fresh dirt sits in the cemetery’s center, marked on either end with flat wooden stakes. Scrawled on one of the stakes is the word sillborn—the t is missing—along with his father’s name. As in other Amish cemeteries in Lancaster County, a white fence surrounds the neatly kept graves, and the headstones are unadorned. It’s everything the public narrative over the boy’s death hasn’t been: simple, modest, and solemn.
The family at the center of Pennsylvania’s measles controversy tells their story.
items.titleTR: The Measles-Stricken Mother Who Lost Her Newborn Son

slots.packetSpot:
It has not yet been determined whether the death of a newborn baby in Lancaster County was connected to measles. While the Amish family believes the mother’s severe measles during pregnancy played a role in the loss, coroner Stephen Diamantoni says he believes the cause of death was a traumatic splenic rupture unrelated to measles; the investigation is ongoing.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro announced the two deaths in the state as “measles-related.” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. criticized that statement and, without presenting evidence, suggested that the deaths may have been fabricated. Amid the family’s grief, the debate unfolding before the medical assessment is complete has become a public struggle over how the deaths are characterized.
slots.packetTitle: A baby's death at the heart of the measles debate

items.descriptionTR: Waymo will begin inviting riders on a rolling basis and slowly ramp up access in the three cities, following its usual commercial playbook.
items.titleTR: Waymo accelerates robotaxi expansion with launches in Denver, San Diego, and Tampa

slots.packetSpot:
Waymo announced that it has begun offering its robotaxi service to the public in Denver, San Diego and Tampa. The company said it would invite riders in stages and gradually expand access; the move brings the number of US cities where it operates commercially to 14.

Waymo's fleet has grown to more than 4,000 vehicles, including a minibus called Ojai. In Denver and San Diego, riders will be offered only Ojai, equipped with Waymo's sixth-generation autonomous driving system. The company's approach in new markets is based on mapping and testing first, then removing the safety operator from the vehicle and opening the service to invitees.

Tesla is reportedly charging for driverless Model Y rides in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa; however, service in some markets is reported to be limited. In Nevada, Tesla and Uber, alongside Waymo, have also received permits. Waymo also plans to launch robotaxi services in London and Munich.
slots.packetTitle: Robotaxis break into new markets

items.descriptionTR:
It was a match between two disjointed sides, two sides trying to carve out new identities following the drop into the Championship. West Ham won thanks to a bit of luck, a degree of resolve and, crucially, a sharpness in front of goal that took them away from Wolves and reduced the pressure on Nuno Espírito Santo, for a few days at least.
First-half goals from Divine Mukasa and Jarrod Bowen, from the penalty spot, were complemented by two more after the interval, as Mukasa secured his second alongside a goal for Konstantinos Mavropanos. The defender doubled up, too, albeit by scoring at his own end, as Wolves tried to claw their way back into contention, and the visitors could also claim a decent goal from Marshall Munetsi. For all their obvious technical ability, however, César Peixoto’s side lacked the hosts’ sang froid at the crucial moments and that proved the decisive factor.
items.titleTR: West Ham fight off Wolves as Divine Mukasa double eases pressure on Nuno

slots.packetSpot:
West Ham United secured their first league win of the Championship season by beating Wolverhampton Wanderers 4-2 at London Stadium on 1 September 2026. Divine Mukasa scored twice, while Jarrod Bowen and Konstantinos Mavropanos also found the net for the home side; Wolves' goals came from Marshall Munetsi and a Mavropanos own goal. The result is reported to have eased the pressure on Nuno Espírito Santo.

Wolves suffered their first defeat under César Peixoto. Peixoto said his team had created numerous scoring opportunities but that he believed a two-goal defeat was unfair. Espírito Santo, meanwhile, stated that the win was a much-needed result, although there were still mistakes that needed to be corrected.

Amanda Staveley, who has been linked to a consortium seeking to acquire a significant stake in West Ham, also watched the match from the stands.
slots.packetTitle: A breath of relief for West Ham

The Madlanga commission has postponed deputy Crime Intelligence head Feroz Khan’s testimony to 28 September, ordering an independent medical assessment amid scrutiny over altered and backdated sick notes.
The Madlanga commission has postponed deputy Crime Intelligence head Feroz Khan’s testimony to 28 September, ordering an independent medical assessment amid scrutiny over altered and backdated sick notes.
items.titleTR: Khan’s sick-note saga delays his testimony at Madlanga commission

slots.packetSpot:
South Africa’s Madlanga Commission postponed the testimony of Crime Intelligence deputy head Feroz Khan to 28 September 2026. The commission asked Khan to submit a sworn statement addressing its questions by 18 September; it said he could be excused from the 28 September hearing only if an independent assessment by an expert agreed upon by 8 September confirms that he is unable to testify.

Khan did not attend the subpoenaed hearing on 1 September. His lawyers said he was recovering following the alleged assassination attempt on 28 June and that he was later reportedly readmitted to Milpark Hospital in Johannesburg. The commission is also questioning medical reports that arose during a labour dispute. According to Adila Hassim, who is leading the presentation of evidence, Khan’s doctor, Dr Fine, submitted a sworn statement admitting that he altered a report at Khan’s son’s request, moving the date on which Khan was deemed fit to return to work from 30 June to 27 June. Khan’s lawyer, Muhammed Vally, said the reports were reviewed after the South African Police Service requested additional information and asked for the medical information to be kept confidential.
slots.packetTitle: The health threshold before testimony

items.descriptionTR: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines on Tuesday against flying into Russian airspace as his military responds to an “escalation” in missile and drone attacks. Zelensky said in an evening address that Russia has recently changed its defense tactics, focusing on strikes from Ukrainian airspace. After the most recent wave of attacks, the Ukrainian president…
items.titleTR: Zelensky warns airlines Russia’s sky ‘completely unsafe’

slots.packetSpot:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines using Russian airspace, insurers and those benefiting from major Russian airports that the airspace is becoming increasingly dangerous. He made this assessment in the context of an escalation in missile and drone attacks and his remarks that Russia has changed its defence tactics.

Zelenskyy said the effects of the war would not remain confined to Ukrainian territory; however, he also stated that Ukraine's threats do not encompass civilian aircraft. He said Ukrainian authorities would inform international organisations about the alleged dangers in Russian airspace.
slots.packetTitle: Zelenskyy's warning over Russian skies

items.descriptionTR:
Jackson Hole is where the world’s central bankers gather every August to think out loud about the global economy. What they say moves markets and shapes rate expectations. This year, it also revealed how much of the global monetary policy debate has become a conversation about the Gulf.
Kevin Warsh, who became US Federal Reserve chairman in May, used his first Jackson Hole speech to signal a policy reset. Inflation remains too high, the Fed has more work to do and the era of the central bank guiding investors through future rate decisions is over.
What he did not say directly is that the price environment the Fed is navigating has been fundamentally shaped by this year's Gulf conflict and its consequences for energy markets. You cannot separate 3.7 per cent PCE (Personal Consumption Expenditures) inflation from Brent crude at $105 a barrel. They are part of the same problem.
Gulf is the inflation story
The International Energy Agency’s Oil Market Report this month found that 8.3 million barrels per day of Gulf output remained effectively shut in, with continuing constraints on Strait of Hormuz oil transit. Global oil inventories fell by 69 million barrels in July.
Brent dropped to $69 a barrel on July 2 following the signing of a deal between the US and Iran, then climbed to $105 on July 23 after renewed attacks on oil tankers. That 52 per cent swing in three weeks reflects a market that has not resolved its fundamental supply question.
Mr Warsh acknowledged this indirectly, noting the “recent rise in overall commodity prices bears watching” and citing possible developments in supply chains, investment flows and geopolitics. The Gulf is the geopolitics to which he was referring.
The UAE’s decision to exit Opec in May placed it in an unusual position. As an independent producer, it has flexibility that Opec members do not. But Hormuz disruption affects Gulf producers regardless of cartel status. The constraint on export routes is geographic, not political.
For the UAE, the current environment creates a revenue windfall alongside infrastructure and routing pressures requiring investment and diplomatic management. The question is what happens to elevated oil revenue when the geopolitical situation stabilises.
What G20 means for the Gulf
That question will be shaped partly by the G20 finance ministers and central bank governors' meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, on Monday and Tuesday.
For Gulf economies, two agenda items have particular relevance: cross-border payment and global imbalance.
Cross-border payment reform is a strategic Gulf interest. The UAE and Saudi Arabia have invested significantly in alternative payment infrastructure to reduce dependence on dollar-clearing systems. Any substantive G20 framework could affect the competitive position of financial hubs including DIFC and Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM.
The global imbalance discussion is more politically charged. While it focuses largely on Chinese industrial overcapacity, Gulf producers face their own structural question: the balance between petrodollar accumulation and domestic absorption capacity and how those surpluses are recycled into global capital markets.
Digital assets are another important signal. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s Finance Track explicitly endorses “a vibrant digital assets ecosystem”. This aligns with the UAE’s positioning as a regulated digital asset hub, where the ADGM and Vara have established frameworks ahead of many G20 economies.
Jackson Hole’s theme this year – Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy – also overlaps with the Asheville agenda. For the UAE, which has made financial infrastructure a sovereign strategic priority, reading those signals together matters.
What Fed reset means for Gulf capital
Mr Warsh’s declaration that forward guidance has overstayed its welcome has specific implications for Gulf sovereign wealth funds and major Gulf Co-operation Council corporate treasuries.
For years, the Fed’s practice of signalling rate intentions allowed sophisticated capital allocators to position ahead of rate cycles. That advantage is being removed.
The next Federal Open Market Committee decision on September 15-16 will therefore be more genuinely uncertain. Gulf capital allocators with significant US fixed-income exposure should treat that uncertainty as real.
The Treasury market adds another layer. The 30-year US Treasury yield recently reached a 19-year high before easing after Mr Bessent announced an expansion of the government’s long-term debt buyback programme.
Gulf sovereign wealth funds are among the largest holders of US Treasury securities. Elevated Gulf oil revenue meeting high US borrowing costs and a volatile long-end yield curve create a more complicated allocation environment than the low-rate decade that preceded it.
Scenario Gulf should prepare for
The most consequential near-term scenario is a partial reopening of Hormuz – sufficient to push Brent towards the $70-$75 range associated with a more normalised supply picture.
That would reduce Gulf oil revenue while the Fed rate environment remains elevated, compressing the window of high revenue and available capital.
The diversification investments the UAE and Saudi Arabia have made in technology, real estate, financial services and manufacturing become more valuable precisely when oil revenue normalises downwards.
Mr Warsh’s message from Jackson Hole is that the Fed will not rescue that scenario with easier money. His commitment is to price stability, not accommodating the capital cycle of commodity exporters.
The period of high oil revenue and easy global money is over. At most, one of those conditions will persist. The Gulf’s strategic bet over the past decade has been on making itself resilient enough not to need both.
Warsh borrowed from General Chuck Yeager to close his argument: “At the moment of truth, there are either reasons or results.”
The old frameworks – Fed forward guidance, stable Hormuz transit, low rates and predictable G20 consensus – are all under pressure simultaneously.
What replaces them is being negotiated now, in Wyoming, North Carolina and in the decisions of sovereign wealth managers across the Gulf. The outcomes are not determined. The moment is.
Andrea Zanon is a senior adviser to entrepreneurs and global leaders, with more than 20 years of experience in economic strategy, market access and geopolitical risk. He contributes a monthly column to The National
items.titleTR: After Jackson Hole, the Gulf is now central to the global rate debate

An assessment published in The National under Andrea Zanon’s byline reads Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s first speech at Jackson Hole as a sign of a shift in monetary policy: it argues that inflation remains high, that the Fed still has work to do, and that guidance on future interest-rate decisions has ended.

According to the article, this debate is intertwined with developments in the Gulf and their pressure on energy prices and inflation. It reports that global oil inventories fell by 69 million barrels in July, that 8.3 million barrels per day of Gulf production was effectively taken offline, and that oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz was restricted. It states that Brent crude fell to $69 on 2 July following the agreement between the United States and Iran, before rising to $105 on 23 July after attacks on oil tankers resumed.

Within this framework, a more complex allocation environment is described for the oil revenues, sovereign wealth funds and exposure to US fixed-income assets of the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The article reports that the Federal Open Market Committee decision on 15-16 September has become more uncertain; that the yield on the 30-year US Treasury bond recently reached a 19-year high; and that it fell after Scott Bessent announced an expansion of the long-term debt buyback programme.

It is assessed that the themes of cross-border payments, global imbalances and digital assets at the G20 meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors to be held in Asheville are also significant for the Gulf. It is argued that Bessent’s support for a “vibrant digital asset ecosystem” aligns with the UAE’s positioning, where ADGM and Vara are establishing regulatory frameworks. The partial reopening of Hormuz and a decline in Brent to the $70-$75 range are presented not as an accomplished outcome, but as a possible scenario for how oil revenues and a high-interest-rate environment could change simultaneously.
slots.packetTitle: The Gulf at the heart of the rate debate

items.descriptionTR: France will start imposing fees on ultra-fast fashion from Tuesday, with charges set to rise to almost €20 per garment as the government steps up pressure on major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein.
items.titleTR: France takes aim at fast-fashion giants with new pricing penalties

slots.packetSpot:
France will begin imposing a charge on clothing in the ultra-fast-fashion category from 1 September 2026, following legislation passed by parliament at the start of the year. The classification is based on the volume of clothing placed on the market and the ratio of repair costs to the purchase price.

The amounts reported for 2026 range from €0.50 for underwear in this category to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for jackets. The charge is expected to be able to rise to €19.50 per item by 2030, provided it does not exceed 50% of the pre-tax price.

French authorities link the rise in low-priced ultra-fast fashion to Shein, Temu and AliExpress. While criticism continues that the regulation may not cover retailers such as H&M and Zara, the ministry said the European Commission’s questions regarding compliance with EU law had been addressed. China had described the regulation as discriminatory in July and warned of possible retaliation.
slots.packetTitle: The price of cheapness

items.descriptionTR: President Trump told reporters Monday in the Oval Office that it’s too early to discuss the possibility of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth running for president in 2028. “I think he’s doing a fantastic job, but it’s very early to talk about that,” Trump said in response to chatter about a Hegseth run. “We have to…
items.titleTR: Trump on talk of Hegseth 2028 run: ‘It’s very early to talk about that’

slots.packetSpot:
Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that it was still too early to discuss the possibility that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could run for president in 2028. Trump said Hegseth was doing a “great job” and added that the midterm elections had to be gotten through first.

NBC News had reported that Hegseth was considering a possible candidacy for 2028. Hegseth, however, called the claim “100 percent false” on X and said it was based on anonymous sources.

Vice President Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Senator Ted Cruz are also being mentioned among possible candidates for 2028. Trump said he thought Cruz could run and that he found him “very talented.”
slots.packetTitle: Too early for 2028

items.descriptionTR:
The words of warning given after Tadej Pogacar's stunning performance on Stage 4 of the Vuelta a Espana turned out to be sadly prophetic for UAE Team Emirates-XRG.
Pogacar had just produced an astonishing solo win in Andorra, with the attack launched 50km from the finish line, which resulted in his overall lead jumping from 9 seconds to 3 minutes 21 seconds. It was the biggest margin of victory of his Grand Tour career. Such was the Slovenian's dominance that it looked like it was game over for his rivals, despite the fact there were still 17 stages to go.
Team boss Matxin Joxean Fernandez was at pains to remind people of that latter fact. “Tadej has made a big statement,” he said. "[But] there's a long way to go, too. Look at the Tour and what happened to Jonas Vingegaard … there was a roundabout, a bend, and suddenly he'd fallen, and he was gone.”
The Spaniard was referring to Stage 15 of the Tour de France when Vingegaard's race ended after he suffered a crash that left him with a broken collarbone and ended his season prematurely.
Fast-forward 41 days, and the dangerous nature of elite-level cycling brutally hit home at La Vuelta as Pogacar hit the deck with just over 30km of Stage 8 left.
The moment that ended Tadej's Vuelta 😕  Tadej Pogačar abandoned La Vuelta a España after this crash on Stage 8 while wearing the red jersey. pic.twitter.com/Un15UcL6mH
— Velon CC (@VelonCC) August 29, 2026
The 27-year-old had been thrown heavily over his handlebars in the middle of the peloton, leaving him with a concussion and, like his old rival Vingegaard, a broken collarbone. His hopes of a first Vuelta crown were over.
“He was leading the race and on course to win the Vuelta a Espana,” said an ashen-faced Fernandez on Friday. “On paper, if something like this hadn’t happened, we had every reason to be optimistic. Unfortunately, though, this is another stone in the road, just like in life generally.”
Teammate Pavel Sivakov described how Pogacar was drinking from his bottle when he hit a small object on the road – with reports suggesting either a rock or a piece of equipment such as a GoPro camera – and lost his balance.
“I was on Tadej's wheel when the crash happened,” said the French rider. “Maybe if you had two hands on the handlebars, it would have been a different crash, because when you lose the bars with one hand, you're really exposed; you cannot really protect yourself.”
On Sunday morning, Pogacar posted a photo of himself on his Instagram Story from his hospital bed in Barcelona, soundtracked by the Bee Gees song Stayin' Alive, in which he wore a neck brace and plasters on wounds on his head and hands.
Beaten up but still the same Tadej 🤘  Tadej Pogačar posted an Instagram Story from his hospital bed on Sunday morning, a day after suffering concussion and fractures to a neck bone and his collarbone in a race-ending crash on Stage 8 of La Vuelta a España.  📸 @TamauPogi pic.twitter.com/ax3xXJmYL4
— Velon CC (@VelonCC) August 30, 2026
Because of his concussion, surgery had to be delayed, but on Monday night the Emirati team announced that Pogacar “underwent successful surgery on his left clavicle” and will remain in hospital to be monitored “for a few days”.
“When ready, Tadej will travel home to begin his recovery and rehabilitation under the supervision of the team’s medical staff. We will continue to monitor his progress closely throughout the recovery process,” UAE Team Emirates-XRG medical director Dr Adrian Rotunno said in a statement.
It remains likely that the six-time Grand Tour champion's season is now over, with Pogacar set to miss out on the chance of winning a third consecutive gold medal in the elite men's race at the Road World Championships, which take place in Montreal on September 27.
Both Fernandez and Pogacar's agent, Alex Carera, insisted over the weekend that no decision has been made and that there would be no rush to make a call. “Only after the surgery is complete will we know exactly how long his recovery will be … In short, let's cross our fingers and wait for the next updates,” Carera told Quibici Sport on Saturday.
If the worst-case scenario emerges and his campaign is over, it will not take the shine off what has been yet another magnificent season in the saddle for Pogacar.
His victories include the Milano-Sanremo, Tour de Romandie, Strade Bianche, Tour of Flanders, Liege-Bastogne-Liege, and a fifth Tour de France title.
In La Vuelta, he had already won three stages and built up a formidable lead of nearly four minutes in the general classification before Friday's crash. His third and final stage win in Spain – which saw Pogacar narrowly avoid crashing out of the race two days before he actually did – took him to 22 victories in 2026.
Pogacar's only other disappointment came in the Paris-Roubaix, when he finished runner-up for the second year running – to Mathieu van der Poel in 2025 and then Wout van Aert in April, when the Belgian came out on top in a gripping sprint finish.
“The big goal remains Paris−Roubaix,” admitted Pogacar, who needs to win the “Hell of the North” to complete a clean sweep of cycling's five Monument races, at the start of August.
With that, La Vuelta, the Itzulia Basque Country and a record-breaking sixth Tour crown – as well as an Olympic gold medal at the 2028 LA Games – still to tick off his to-do list, there are plenty of goals left before Pogacar decides to call it a day, although that horror fall on Saturday provided a stark reminder that riders do not necessarily get the final say in that decision.
items.titleTR: Tadej Pogacar has 'successful surgery' after Vuelta crash but season finale remains under threat

slots.packetSpot:
UAE Team Emirates-XRG announced that Tadej Pogačar, who withdrew from La Vuelta after crashing on Stage 8, successfully underwent surgery on his left collarbone. According to the team’s statement, after leaving the hospital in Barcelona, where he will remain under observation for several days, Pogačar will begin a recovery and rehabilitation process under the supervision of the medical team.

It was reported that Pogačar, who had won three stages while leading the race, fractured his collarbone and suffered a concussion in the crash. Pavel Sivakov said that Pogačar hit a small object on the road while drinking from his bottle; it was not clarified whether the object was a rock or equipment such as a GoPro.

His participation in the Road World Championships to be held in Montreal on 27 September, as well as the rest of his season, remains uncertain. Team boss Matxin Joxean Fernandez and his manager Alex Carera stated that no decision would be made before the recovery period becomes clear.
slots.packetTitle: From the lead to recovery

items.descriptionTR:
At least five people were killed when munitions exploded while being transferred from a vehicle to a warehouse in north-west Syria on Tuesday, underscoring the danger posed by the proliferation of weapons in the country after almost 14 years of civil war.
Shells, ammunition and other military ordnance inside the vehicle were detonated in Binnish, in Idlib governorate, official news agency Sana reported.
According to a local source, the detonations began while the munitions were being unloaded from a vehicle at the warehouse of an arms dealer, who was killed in the blasts.
The explosions continued for more than an hour and a half, destroying some shops in the area.
Sobhi Assaf, an official at the Health Ministry in Idlib, told The National at least five people had been killed and added that the death toll was not final.
Civil defence teams were still searching for missing people and securing the scene of the blast, he said.
Mustafa Droubi, whose home is close to the site of the explosion, said he saw “bullets flying through the air” and thick smoke.
“I saw human remains as I was heading to work,” he told The National. “It was a very powerful explosion. There were shells that had not yet exploded.”
￼
Authorities have not said who was in the vehicle or why the ammunition exploded.
Idlib province was a rebel stronghold during the civil war, with many weapon depots in the area and much of the population heavily armed.
Rebel forces led by Hayat Tahrir Al Sham, a former Al Qaeda affiliate, launched an 11-day offensive in December 2024 that ultimately toppled the regime of Bashar Al Assad. The group's former members now control the state.
items.titleTR: Explosions in north-west Syria kill at least five

According to Sana, shells, ammunition and other military materials in the vehicle exploded.
