Artificial intelligence is becoming part of institutions’ decisions on governance, curricula and teaching arrangements, rather than merely a tool used in the classroom. A commentary from South Africa treats schools’ approach to artificial intelligence as a governance test in terms of written rules, data management, teacher training and communication with parents.

As the 2026-27 academic year begins in the UAE, artificial intelligence literacy was reported to have been incorporated into the curriculum in line with the Ministry of Education’s guidance on the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence in the classroom. At Muna British Academy, it was stated that artificial intelligence-related content would be covered across lessons alongside coding, robotics and computer science.

Macquarie University in Australia, meanwhile, incorporated a chatbot called Virtual Peer into online learning activities in two compulsory psychology courses. While the university says the tool does not replace instructors and that optional human feedback sessions continue, some students and academics are voicing concerns about reduced face-to-face contact and the role of staff. Face-to-face classes are planned to be offered again in alternating terms from 2027.
slots.packetTitle: AI moves into education's institutional core

items.descriptionTR: As the steep decline in student enrollment continues at the start of the 2026 school year, the Education Ministry and local authorities are seeking new planning strategies to prevent 'school deserts.'
items.titleTR: French schools face 'unprecedented challenge' of accelerating demographic decline

items.descriptionTR: Since 2024, the federal government and the government of Québec have tightened immigration rules, leading to a drop in enrollment at the country's higher education institutions, weakening their finances and raising fears of longer-term damage to Canada's appeal.
items.titleTR: International students turn away from Canadian universities as immigration rules tighten

items.descriptionTR: The recent release of A-level and GSCE data for UK students and schools has renewed calls to ‘revitalise arts education’
items.titleTR: Art and design A-levels at lowest uptake since 2010 according to UK advocacy group

slots.packetSpot:
As demographic decline reduces the number of pupils in schools in France, tightened immigration policies in Canada and Québec are narrowing international student admissions. In the United Kingdom, meanwhile, the share of art and design A-level applications in the total is declining.

According to estimates by France’s Ministry of Education, around 161,000 fewer pupils will enter primary, middle and high schools at the start of the 2026 academic year than in 2025. The ministry’s projection points to a loss of 1.7 million pupils over the next decade, equivalent to around 15 percent of the current total. It is reported that more than 5,000 schools have closed since 2012, 400 of them since 2024. In rural areas, school closures are bringing travel times for pupils and the possibility of “school deserts” to the fore.

It is reported that, from 2024 onwards, the federal government and the government of Québec tightened immigration policies in Canada; Ottawa imposed an annual cap on study permits and made admission requirements more stringent. New international student admissions fell from around 125,000 in the first half of 2024 to around 22,000 in the same period of 2026. As of the end of 2024, foreign students accounted for 60 percent of master’s students and around 70 percent of doctoral students at Polytechnique Montréal.

According to an analysis by Campaign for the Arts in the United Kingdom, the share of art and design A-level applications fell from 5.4 percent in 2010 to 4.7 percent in 2026; the share of all arts subjects in A-level applications also declined to 10 percent. While arts subjects accounted for 7 percent of GCSE applications, the figure was 13.4 percent in 2010. By contrast, the share of GCSE art and design rose slightly from 3.35 percent in 2025 to 3.41 percent in 2026.
slots.packetTitle: Narrowing paths into education

items.descriptionTR:
International airlines are continuing to adjust schedules for Middle East flights as airspace restrictions and operational uncertainty persist.
Against the backdrop of continuing geopolitical uncertainty across the region, here's how international airlines are adapting their operations.
Virgin Atlantic
Virgin Atlantic flights to Dubai remain suspended until October 2027, with tickets for the resumed service to go on sale later this year, the airline says in a notice on its website.
“If you're looking to travel sooner, you can still book a Dubai holiday with Virgin Atlantic Holidays, flying with Emirates,” it added.
Air Canada
Air Canada has extended the suspension of its flights to Tel Aviv and Dubai until “mid-January 2027”. Passengers affected by the cancellations are advised to check directly with the airline for rebooking and refund options as schedules continue to be adjusted.
“If you are in either of these regions, please do not head to the airport unless you have a confirmed flight with another airline, and your flight is operating as scheduled. Your safety is our top priority,” the airline said on its website.
Finnair
￼
Finnair has extended the suspension of its flights to both Dubai and Doha until March 27, 2027.
“Finnair continuously monitors the security situation in different regions and, when necessary, makes changes to flight routes or operations. The security situation in the Middle East has remained unstable, with no clear signs of improvement,” the airline said.
KLM
￼
KLM has adjusted its flight schedule across the Middle East and continues to avoid the airspace of Iran, Iraq and Israel, as well as parts of the Arabian Gulf.
The airline has resumed services to Tel Aviv, with flights stopping in Larnaca, Cyprus, where crews will rest overnight.
“We always check the situation and adjust our flights to keep you safe and give you the best options,” the airline said.
Flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam and Dubai remain suspended until October 24.
Passengers affected by cancellations can rebook their journeys for a later date or request a refund, depending on their ticket conditions.
Air France
Air France has resumed its regular flights to Dubai and Riyadh, but flights to Beirut remain suspended until September 13.
"The company continuously monitors the geopolitical situation in the territories served and overflown by its aircraft in order to ensure the highest level of flight safety and security," the airline said.
Wizz Air
Wizz Air services from mainland Europe to Amman are suspended until ⁠September 21 while flights to Dubai and Abu Dhabi are suspended until October 24.
Singapore Airlines
￼
Singapore Airlines flights to Dubai were scheduled to resume on August 2, but the suspension has been extended until October 24.
“As the situation remains fluid, other flights may be affected,” the airline said on its website. “Customers affected by flight cancellations will be reaccommodated on alternative flights or can seek a full refund of the unused portion of their ticket.”
Scoot
The low-cost subsidiary of Singapore Airlines has suspended its Singapore-Jeddah flights until September 12.
Customers affected by flight cancellations may request a full refund if they choose not to continue with their travel, or rebook on alternative Scoot flights, the airline said.
Turkish Airlines
Turkish Airlines has resumed flights to Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Damascus, Beirut and Amman as the carrier continues to restore services across parts of the Middle East. But flights to Tehran remain suspended. The airline also warned of further disruption due to the latest escalation.
“Some of our flights to and from Iran and the surrounding region have been cancelled. The current situation in the region's airspace is being monitored in real-time, and additional flight cancellations may occur,” the airline posted on its website.
Philippine Airlines
Philippine Airlines flights from Manila to Doha have resumed, but flights to Dubai are suspended until October 2.
“We continue to closely monitor the situation and will restore full capacity as conditions allow,” the airline said.
British Airways
British Airways has delayed its phased return to the Middle East. Under the revised schedule, flights to Dubai, Tel Aviv, Bahrain and Amman will remain suspended until October 25.
The carrier has also reduced frequencies on other Middle East routes, for example, to Doha and Riyadh, and has suspended flights to Jeddah.
Air Astana
Kazakhstan's national carrier had earlier suspended flights from Almaty and Astana to Dubai until August 31 “due to the further deterioration of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf area”.
But flights between the cities are now to remain cancelled until at least September 30. “Passengers are entitled to a full refund at the point of purchase, free rebooking to later dates, or rebooking to other international destinations operated by Air Astana,” the airline said.
Cathay Pacific
The Hong Kong carrier has extended its suspension of flights to and from Dubai and Riyadh until October 25 and October 26, respectively. Flights had been scheduled to resume on September 1.
“Affected travellers will be offered the flexibility to rebook, reroute or refund their tickets. Cathay will continue to closely monitor the evolving situation in the Middle East,” the airline said.
Lufthansa
Lufthansa Group has suspended flights to several destinations in the region.
While Austrian Airlines, Lufthansa and Swiss have resumed operations to Tel Aviv, Brussels Airlines flights to Tel Aviv remain suspended.
Lufthansa and Swiss flights to Dubai also remain suspended until September 13.
Meanwhile, services of Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian Airlines and Brussels Airlines to Abu Dhabi, Amman, Beirut, Dammam, Riyadh, Erbil, Muscat and Tehran are on hold until October 24.
ITA Airways
The national carrier of Italy has suspended flights to Riyadh until September 15, while flights to Dubai are suspended until October 24.
“Passengers can request rebooking on an alternative flight or a refund of their ticket,” the airline said.
United Airlines
United Airlines flights to Dubai and Tel Aviv continue to be affected by continuing disruption.
Passengers affected by cancellations until September 7 can rebook their travel or request a refund, depending on ticket conditions, the airline said.
American Airlines
American Airlines has updated its travel alerts for passengers flying to or through parts of the Middle East, including Tel Aviv and Doha, with flexible booking options in place.
Customers who bought tickets before March 28 for travel between February 28 and January 6, 2027, can make a one-time change without a fee, provided they keep the same origin and destination and travel in the same cabin, subject to availability.
Passengers also have the option to cancel their trip and request a refund, depending on ticket conditions. The airline said schedules and policies remain subject to change.
Delta
Delta flights between Tel Aviv and several US cities including Atlanta, Boston and New York remain suspended until December 18.
AirBaltic
Flights operated by the Latvian flag carrier between Riga and Dubai remain suspended until October 24.
Korean Air
Korean Air's regular service between Incheon and Dubai remains suspended, with no date set for flights to resume.
“As limited airspace capacity related to the conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran continues, the suspension of the Incheon-Dubai route will be extended until further notice,” the airline said.
“A decision on when to resume flights will be made at a later date, following a comprehensive review of Dubai Airport's normalisation and market demand recovery.”
items.titleTR: Middle East flights: Which airlines are flying and which remain suspended?

items.descriptionTR: Air travel in Austria has seen several challenges this year. We look at the planned cuts from Austrian Airlines, and some of the other changes to the upcoming winter schedule.
items.titleTR: Cuts, cancelled routes and new schedules: What's changing for flights to and from Austria

slots.packetSpot:
International airlines serving the Middle East are suspending, resuming, reducing or rerouting their flights because of airspace restrictions, security concerns and operational uncertainty. While the situation at destinations such as Dubai, Tel Aviv, Doha, Riyadh, Beirut, Amman, Abu Dhabi and Tehran varies by airline and even by route, many companies are announcing rebooking or refund options for passengers.

Austrian Airlines, meanwhile, plans to scale back its winter schedule, citing high fuel costs and economic losses that the company links to the Iran conflict. According to the company's statement, the Vienna–Graz route will be discontinued; flights to Tbilisi, Keflavik and Porto will also be suspended for the time being. Networks are being reshaped not only by cancellations, but also by additional connections to some hubs and the entry of other carriers.
slots.packetTitle: Flight networks are being redrawn

items.descriptionTR: Physicists have mathematically captured a bizarre “spacetime crystal” that can either dissolve or collapse into a microscopic black hole after only a tiny change in energy. Their breakthrough came from an unusual trick involving infinitely many dimensions, potentially giving researchers a new tool for studying primordial and microscopic black holes.
items.titleTR: This strange “spacetime crystal” can suddenly become a black hole

items.descriptionTR: Hawking radiation causes black holes to eventually evaporate. This is because particle pairs are spontaneously created near the event horizon (the position of the last ray of light that can escape the black hole's gravitational pull). A particle and its antiparticle are created for a brief moment and disappear immediately afterward. But sometimes a particle falls into the black hole, allowing the other particle to escape: This is Hawking radiation. According to Stephen Hawking, this would ultimately mean that no black holes would remain in the universe.
items.titleTR: Switching gravity on and off leaves particles behind, mathematical model finds

slots.packetSpot: Two theoretical studies related to black holes mathematically address different consequences of changes in gravitational conditions. A study by researchers at Goethe University Frankfurt and TU Wien examines the possibility that an unstable “crystal” structure formed by spacetime in a critical state may dissolve or collapse into a microscopic black hole with the addition of a small amount of energy. The other model, in the context of Hawking radiation, considers one of the particle–antiparticle pairs said to form near the event horizon escaping while the other falls into the black hole; according to Stephen Hawking, this process may ultimately leave no black holes behind.
slots.packetTitle: Two equations at the edge of a black hole

items.descriptionTR:
Die Abnehmspritze Wegovy bekommt Konkurrenz aus dem eigenen Haus: Der Wirkstoff Semaglutid ist jetzt auch als Tablette erhältlich. Experten warnen vor einem Hype um das vermeintliche Wundermittel. Von Philipp Wundersee.
￼   Die Abnehmspritze Wegovy bekommt Konkurrenz aus dem eigenen Haus: Der Wirkstoff Semaglutid ist jetzt auch als Tablette erhältlich. Experten warnen vor einem Hype um das vermeintliche Wundermittel. Von Philipp Wundersee.[mehr]
items.titleTR: Abnehmspritze Wegovy auch als Pille - die Nebenwirkungen bleiben

items.descriptionTR: Unfortunately, testing hunger neurons in a living person isn't possible, but the study's authors hope their data can guide researchers toward new weight loss treatments.
items.titleTR: GLP-1s may work by activating an unlikely weight loss ally

slots.packetSpot:
As GLP-1 drugs move beyond injections, the conditions of use, side effects and limitations of the semaglutide tablet are also being discussed. Wegovy tablets, available by prescription in Germany from 1 September, are intended for adults with obesity and certain groups of patients with accompanying conditions; as a rule, patients themselves bear the cost of treatment.

In studies reported by Tagesschau, participants who used oral semaglutide alongside a low-calorie diet and more exercise lost an average of around 14 percent of their body weight over 64 weeks. With the weekly injection, this figure rose to as much as 19 percent over 72 weeks. The tablet is taken daily and absorption of the active ingredient through the intestine is lower; according to Hans Hauner, only around 1.5 percent of semaglutide in pill form reaches the bloodstream.

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation and abdominal pain are among the reported side effects. Hauner states that side effects occur in nearly half of those receiving treatment; Ulrike Becker and Hauner draw attention to use without medical supervision, malnutrition and the possibility of regaining weight after stopping the medication.

A mouse study published in PNAS in July by Yale researchers suggests that semaglutide may have increased fat burning at rest by activating AgRP neurons associated with hunger. Mice deprived of these neurons lost less weight and had greater difficulty maintaining weight loss over the long term. Since AgRP neurons cannot currently be tested in living humans, it cannot be said that the findings explain how the process works in humans; the researchers believe this could guide work on treatments that are more effective or have fewer side effects.
slots.packetTitle: A new face of weight-loss medicine

items.descriptionTR:
In Alaska, the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the Alps, deadly chain reactions are just waiting to be triggered
You may not have felt it, but the earth beneath our feet is getting twitchier, and global heating is to blame. As temperatures surge and climate breakdown accelerates, interactions between climate and geology are becoming ever more apparent – as marked by last week’s horrific events in Nepal and Tibet. We still have a bit of a blind spot when it comes to the idea that a changing climate can impact what scientists call the geosphere, but the evidence has long been incontestable.
In 2021, a similar deluge ripped through a series of mountain valleys in the Indian Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, severely damaging two hydroelectric power plants and taking about 200 lives. In August 2025, a colossal landslide in an Alaskan fjord created a 500-metre-high wave in an area frequented by cruise ships. A few months earlier, the collapse of part of a glacier in Switzerland’s Valais canton caused a debris-laden torrent that destroyed and buried most of the already evacuated village of Blatten.
Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at UCL. His latest book is The Fate of the World – a History and Future of the Climate Crisis
items.titleTR: The Nepal and Tibet flood is a warning: melting snow and ice will bring more disasters around the world |  Bill McGuire

items.descriptionTR: Mountainous regions across the planet are warming especially fast, melting the ice that glues rocky slopes and glaciers together
items.titleTR: Mountain warming means there will be more disasters like the Nepal flood

slots.packetSpot:
The sudden flooding reported in Tibet and Nepal on 26 August brought concerns to the fore about growing risks linked to changes in mountain ice and frozen ground. Initial assessments of the event described a glacier break-off, while satellite images obtained later are reported to indicate that an entire slope collapsed together with the rocks around and beneath the glacier. The rock and ice that descended into the valley are said to have created a wave of water and debris; how the floodwater reached such a large volume has not yet been fully clarified.

According to experts, the Himalayas are warming rapidly; the thinning and retreat of glaciers may weaken the structure supporting slopes, while the thawing of frozen ground may reduce the ice holding rock masses together. The number, size and volume of glacial lakes are also increasing. The role of these processes in the disaster in question has not been established; nevertheless, researchers warn that rapid warming in high mountain areas could increase the risk of cascading events such as floods, landslides and debris flows.

The destruction, losses and rescue efforts reported in Nepal also made the human dimension of this risk visible. Steps are being taken in India to establish early warning systems against glacial lake outburst floods; experts draw attention to the importance of monitoring, scientific investigation and the participation of local communities in mountainous terrain.
slots.packetTitle: The mountains' unraveling balance

items.descriptionTR:
￼
The lives that slither and scurry beneath the soil’s surface are vital for ecological health: now we can listen in to them
- by Ella Browning
Read on Aeon
items.titleTR: Worm munch matters

items.descriptionTR: More than 1,000 volunteers buried cotton underwear across Switzerland to help scientists measure how active different soils are. The faster the fabric disappeared, the more biological activity was taking place underground. Gardens showed the fastest decomposition, while lawns had the least, revealing how strongly land management can shape soil life.
items.titleTR: Why scientists asked 1,000 people to bury their underwear

slots.packetSpot:
Life underground is being tracked through the unusual traces it leaves, even if it cannot be seen directly. In studies reported by Ella Browning, acoustic sensors buried in soil record sounds produced by activities such as worms’ movement and feeding. Although initial findings suggest that sound patterns may be linked to soil conditions and biodiversity, the sources of these sounds need to be distinguished and the effects of moisture and soil type need to be taken into account.

In Switzerland, the Proof by Underpants project run by the University of Zurich and Agroscope used the rate at which cotton underwear decomposes as an accessible indicator of underground biological activity. Land use was reported to have the strongest effect among the factors examined in relation to decomposition. Even so, rapid decomposition is not considered a positive sign in every ecosystem; in environments such as forests and gardens, it can also point to disruptions in nutrient balance.
slots.packetTitle: The traces of life beneath the soil

items.descriptionTR:
Southern Africa is bracing for a very strong El Niño this summer, developing earlier than usual and set to peak between October and January, though experts caution precise regional impacts remain uncertain.
Southern Africa is bracing for a very strong El Niño this summer, developing earlier than usual and set to peak between October and January, though experts caution precise regional impacts remain uncertain.
items.titleTR: Very strong El Niño forecast for southern Africa this summer

items.descriptionTR:
“One more warning sign here of what we're facing in a warmer world.”
Every few years, El Niño or its cool counterpart, La Niña, shifts rainfall across the tropics, dries out Australia, floods parts of Peru, and rearranges the weather on most of the planet. The two are the warm and cold swings of a single system, the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, and that system is the largest source of year-to-year climate variation on Earth. Its swings sit atop the steadily rising temperatures driven by global warming.
But we didn't know whether global warming was making it stronger. It’s possible that the added energy in the atmosphere and oceans was causing its swings to be more dramatic.
“We've been seeing some very strong El Niño events in the late 20th and early 21st century, and what we didn't know was how unusual those are,” said Julie Cole, an environmental scientist at the University of Michigan. Because models disagree with one another and the instrumental data are too short to separate a trend, Cole’s team reconstructed a thousand-year-long ocean surface temperature record by analyzing fossilized Galápagos corals.
Read full article
Comments
items.titleTR: El Niño is now stronger than at any point in the last 1,000 years, study finds

items.descriptionTR:
￼
The El Niño weather pattern won't peak for several months, but some effects are noticeable right now — both in terms of weather and human preparation. Here's a photographic look at some of the ways El Niño is already making its mark.
items.titleTR: Seabirds, silting and salt: Photos show some of the early effects of El Niño

items.descriptionTR:
Top politicians and scientists blamed the deadly fires on the climate crisis and said it should inspire more emissions reductions and adaptation measures
The post UN chief warns climate crisis “in overdrive” as El Niño threatens to fuel the fire appeared first on Climate Home News.
The United Nations Secretary-General and foreign ministers from the UK, France and Spain have blamed the deadly wildfires engulfing Europe on climate change, using the disaster to renew calls for faster cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.
António Guterres told journalists on Friday that the “climate crisis is in overdrive”, adding that global heat seen so far is just a “warm up act” as a phenomenon known as El Niño intensifies “adding fuel to a planet already on fire”.
A new World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) report published on Friday predicts that the weather pattern will grow into a “strong event” between now and October, increasing the risk of higher than normal temperatures across much of the world and disrupted rainfalls.
“That risks shattering every seasonal record – and driving even more severe effects worldwide,” Guterres said.
El Niño builds on top of an already warming world, driven primarily by the burning of fossil fuels. A WMO scientist, who did not want to be named, told journalists that all the heatwaves and other climate impacts seen so far this year are “before the effects of El Niño are really kicking in at a global scale”.
Fossil fuellling the fires
Fires have broken out across much of Europe but are threatening the most people in the south-west of France near Bordeaux and in Central Spain near Madrid. Nearly a quarter of a million people have been evacuated in France with hundreds of homes destroyed while in Spain 80,000 people have had to leave their homes and at least 13 died in one village.
A scientific study published on Friday by the World Weather Attribution group found that man-made climate change made deadly fires in France twice as likely and those in Spain twenty times more likely. Smaller fires in the UK were not analysed by the study.
UN Climate Change leader Simon Stiell blamed fossil fuels for the fires, as well as storms in Chile and heatwaves in North America and Japan in recent weeks. “The climate alarm is blaring”, he said on Wednesday.
Guterres criticised new fossil fuel production projects and fossil fuel subsidies for causing hardship across the world. Discussing his speech, a senior UN official – who did not want to be named – said the subsidies amounted to trillions of US dollars a year and criticised pension funds and institutional investors, including insurance companies, for continuing to invest in fossil fuel projects.
￼
The head of the United Nations Antonio Guterres (right) with the head of the UN’s climate arm Simon Stiell (left) at COP30 (Photo: Kiara Worth/UNFCCC)
Asked why world leaders and the public are not prioritising climate action, Guterres said they are distracted by wars in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan and elsewhere and sometimes forget “other aspects that are a sometimes even more dangerous threat”.
Also the fossil fuel industry and “some countries” are campaigning to pretend that climate change does not exist, he said, adding that the UN should be more active in “naming the situations as they are and the responsibilties as they are and mobilising the public opinion”.
After meetings in Paris and Madrid earlier in the week, the UK’s new foreign minister Ed Miliband issued joint statements with his French and Spanish counterparts – Jean-Noël Barrot and José Manuel Albares Bueno – calling on the world to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels.
They promised to do more to reduce emissions and protect their people and encouraged other governments to do the same. 
The UK-French statement called on governments to publish UN climate plans, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs), which are aligned with the Paris Agreement’s goal to limit global average temperatures to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.
According to Climate Action Tracker, only three countries – the UK, Nigeria and Norway – have submitted NDCs with 2035 emissions reduction targets which are compatible with 1.5C. Fifty-two countries – including Egypt, Vietnam and Argentina – have yet to submit an NDC at all.
Defending science
Beyond action on emissions, the ministers also intervened in an ongoing dispute over the timing of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC)’s next flagship assessment.
Miliband and Barrot’s statement said they “underline the importance” of that scientific report feeding into governments’ next global stocktake of progress on climate action in two years’ time, calling it a “critical input” to that process.
The timing of this report has been a contentious issue in government negotiations at the IPCC and at June’s climate talks in Bonn. While a group of nations calling themselves the “friends of science” want the report before the stocktake, others like Saudi Arabia and India have argued that this would make the report of a worse quality and less inclusive of developing countries’ scientists.
Science ‘under attack’ from fossil fuel interests at UN climate talks
The UK-Spanish statement weighed in less explicitly on this issue but said that they “recall the importance of scientific evidence and acknowledge the work of the IPCC in this respect.”
The British and French ministers said they would seek to accelerate reductions of emissions in methane, a particularly potent greenhouse gas, at COP31 in November. They encouraged governments “to work jointly to develop a marketplace for fossil fuels with near-zero methane intensity.” 
Methane leaks from oil, gas and coal production are a major contributor to global warming. Over a 20-year period, methane traps around 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide.
￼
Ed Miliband meets José Manuel Albares Bueno in Madrid on 29 July 2026. (Picture by Ed Morris / FCDO)
The UK and Spanish statement emphasised the importance of supporting the Global South and underlined the need to mobilise sustainable financing “at scale with the challenge we face”. The previous UK government, in which Miliband was energy minister, cut climate finance to developing countries to pay for increases in military spending.
The UK government led by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has yet to outline any major changes to climate finance in its two weeks in power but has announced it will convert some finance from grants to loans in order to free up money to subsidise bus travel in England.
More adaptation needed
Guterres said that “it is time to stop treating each disaster as an isolated tragedy and recognise the systemic risk that is unfolding before our eyes.” A recent study found that three-quarters of UK media reports about the British June heatwave did not mention climate change.
As well as reducing emissions, the UN Secretary-General called for measures to adapt vulnerable people to extreme heat. Specifically, he said that buildings should be built and retrofitted for extreme heat and that every city and country should have heat-health action plans and early warning systems. Over 250 cities have joined the UN’s ‘beat the heat’ initiative, he said.
The Portuguese diplomat called for governments and employers to do more to protect their workers from heat, criticising global fashion brands for not setting heat standards for the factories that supply them. “No one should have to risk their life to earn a living,” he said.
items.titleTR: UN chief warns climate crisis “in overdrive” as El Niño threatens to fuel the fire

slots.packetSpot:
The developing El Niño stands out for its unusual strength in forecasts and, in long-term research based on Galápagos corals, for rising variability in the eastern Pacific. While expectations of a very strong event persist for Southern Africa, early signs and preparations from Panama to Indonesia are heightening concerns over how drought, heat, rainfall patterns and wildfire risks may become intertwined in a warmer climate.

The expert group in Southern Africa reports that warming in the Niño 3.4 region began earlier than average; the event could peak between October 2026 and January 2027. However, it stresses that local outcomes remain uncertain because of the distinctive characteristics of each El Niño and other ocean-atmosphere processes.

The study associated with Julie Cole of the University of Michigan reconstructed roughly a thousand years of eastern Pacific temperature variability from fossilized Galápagos corals. Researchers interpret the findings as indicating human influence, saying variability has been 36.5 percent higher since 1984 than in the 1000–1850 period and 16.2 percent higher than in the 1851–1982 period. It is also noted that the evidence for the central Pacific is more uncertain.

The WMO’s assessment draws attention to the risk of above-normal temperatures and disrupted rainfall patterns across large parts of the world, with the possibility of a strong El Niño through October. UN officials warn that an intensifying El Niño could increase pressure in an already warmed world, while reiterating calls for emissions reductions and adaptation to extreme heat.
slots.packetTitle: El Niño's signal in a warming world

items.descriptionTR:
New features are rolling out across the Android ecosystem starting today.
Let's be frank: Some of Google's recent Android feature Drops have been duds, offering little more than an expansion of Gemini summaries and chat functions. The new September Drop does have some Gemini flavor, but there are non-AI goodies, too. Your messaging threads are getting prettier and more useful, and those nifty Motion Assist dots that began appearing last week are rolling out widely. And even the Gemini expansion is not without utility.
Since this is an Android Drop rather than a Pixel Drop, these features are coming to a wider range of devices. The OS version does matter, though. If you're on Android 16 or higher, you can now tell Gemini to log the location of items that don't have a tracker tag attached. Just tell the AI where you put something, and include a photo if you like.
Remembered items in Find Hub

Remembered items in Find Hub
This information will be logged in Find Hub, which has thus far been used for locating phones, earbuds, and tracker tags. You can ask Gemini to recall that information or simply check Find Hub yourself the next time you forget where you put that item.
Read full article
Comments
items.titleTR: New Android Drop adds remembered items in Find Hub, makes anti-nausea dots official

slots.packetSpot:
Google is preparing to add a new memory function to Find Hub on devices running Android 16 and above. Users will be able to tell Gemini where they left an item without a tracking tag and, if they wish, add a photo; this information can later be recalled through Gemini or from Find Hub.

Until now, Find Hub has been used to find phones, headphones and tracking tags. The new function does not automatically track the item's location; it saves the location information provided by the user. Google says the features will soon come to a wider range of Android devices; full availability may take days or weeks.
slots.packetTitle: Find Hub gives forgotten items a memory

items.descriptionTR: The boom of data centers to power artificial intelligence was a topic of discussion at the G20 summit on Tuesday in North Carolina. Elon Musk told member countries that US companies need to find new energy sources outside of China to power these massive data centers. That same issue is also creating a backlash in the United States ahead of the midterm elections in November. Donald Trump is doubling down, calling those who are against the data centers, “backwards and poor.” FRANCE 24's Monte Francis explains.
items.titleTR: AI data centers become surprise issue in US midterm elections

items.descriptionTR: GOP Rep. Tim Burchett (Tenn.) responded on Monday to President Trump’s statement that communities that oppose data center construction want to “end up being backwards and poor.” “I guess I’m backwards and poor,” he told MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez on the House steps.  The Tennessee Republican suggested data centers could be built in military installations instead…
items.titleTR: House Republican pushes back on Trump data center support: ‘I guess I’m backwards and poor’

slots.packetSpot:
Donald Trump supports the expansion of AI data centres in the United States and describes those opposing these projects as “backward and poor.” As the November midterm elections approach, the debate has moved onto the political agenda, while Republican Representative Tim Burchett of Tennessee responded to those remarks by saying, “I guess I’m backward and poor.”

Burchett said data centres could be built at military facilities rather than in residential areas, and that local oversight and consultation with relevant parties should be strengthened. In a Fox News poll conducted last month, 70 percent of respondents opposed the construction of a data centre in their area; the figure was recorded at 60 percent among Republicans and 76 percent among Democrats. Environmental and financial burdens, water use and pressure on the electricity grid are cited among the main reasons for the objections.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott imposed a moratorium on new data-centre construction over concerns about water use and grid strain. Republican Representative Thomas Massie also called for regulatory and decision-making authority at the local level. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, meanwhile, placed scepticism towards data centres in the context of competition with China; he said Republicans were investigating whether China had a role in spreading misinformation. Speaking at the G20 meeting in North Carolina, Elon Musk also stated that US companies need to find new sources outside China to power large AI data centres.
slots.packetTitle: Data centres at the ballot box

items.descriptionTR:
It is the second round of strikes after nearly a month of no military action.
The U.S. on Tuesday launched a new series of strikes against Iranian targets, as peace talks remain stalled and President Donald Trump continues to express his frustration with Iranian leadership.
Trump on Tuesday called the strikes “large and powerful” and warned Iran against any retaliatory strikes.
“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!” Trump said in a post to social media.
In a post announcing the attacks, U.S. Central Command said they “follow recent attempted attacks by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.”
The two rounds of strikes the U.S. launched this week mark a renewed exchange of fire between the two countries after a weekslong pause in fighting. The administration also announced last week “Operation Economic Outcast,” a new effort that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said will economically isolate Iran.
Trump’s threat is a sharp pivot from earlier this week, when CENTCOM described strikes on Iran’s Larak Island as “limited, precise action.” Those strikes, Iran’s state-run media reported, killed at least two and wounded several others.
Ahead of Tuesday’s strikes, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country was ready to return to the since-expired ceasefire agreement if the U.S. was.
“I am stating clearly that if the U.S. returns to its commitments under the Memorandum of Understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian  said at a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, according to state-run media.
Trump has publicly expressed frustration with Iranian leadership, writing on social media on Monday that their “leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country.”
items.titleTR: US launches ‘large and powerful’ new strikes at Iran

slots.packetSpot:
New US airstrikes on targets in Iran, along with missile and drone attacks that Iran presented as retaliation, are once again deepening the security and maritime shipping crisis around the Strait of Hormuz. Some of Iran’s claims that US facilities in Jordan, Bahrain and Iraq were targeted have not been independently verified; according to initial information on the attack in Jordan, two US officials said there were no fatalities.

Tanker traffic and energy exports from the Gulf fell sharply after it was reported that two tankers leaving Hormuz had been struck. According to the Iranian Red Crescent, five people were killed and 50 injured at a wedding near Sirik on the coast of the strait. While Donald Trump linked the new attacks to Iran’s attempts to lay naval mines in the strait and missiles fired at the US base in Jordan, the Revolutionary Guards argued that the US attacks would increase pressure on the strait. Scott Bessent also said Washington could announce new sanctions against Iran this week.
slots.packetTitle: Fire returns to Hormuz

items.descriptionTR:
Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz
The US and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates in response.
The US president, Donald Trump, on Monday threatened further action. The US is trying to prise open Tehran’s grip on shipping going through the strait, which before the war accounted for a fifth of the world’s seaborne energy supply. Washington claimed that Iranian control over the waterway had been loosened by repeated US attacks on Iranian missile launchers and radars.
items.titleTR: Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up

slots.packetSpot:
For the first time in a month, reciprocal attacks between the United States and Iran were reported again. Washington said it had struck two Iranian missile launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz and detected that Iran was preparing to lay mines in the strait. Iran's Revolutionary Guards, meanwhile, claimed to have targeted US-operated bases in Jordan with ballistic missiles, causing heavy damage; the United States said missiles directed at its forces in Jordan had been intercepted without significant impact. The United Arab Emirates also announced that it had intercepted a drone over its territorial waters.

Iran claimed that three of its soldiers had been killed and two of its citizens wounded in the US attack, and that its air defences had shot down a US MQ-9 drone. Donald Trump said there would be a response, threatening to take further steps after Iran's retaliation.

The sides' accounts conflict over control and transit security in the Strait of Hormuz. While Iran warned that ships violating its rules would face the same fate, Washington argues that Iranian control in the strait has weakened. US sanctions pressure on Iran also continues.
slots.packetTitle: The Strait of Hormuz returns to the line of fire

items.descriptionTR:
During a White House meeting last week, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll brought his concerns about the future of the Army under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directly to President Trump—a sign of how far tensions between the two Pentagon leaders had escalated, and of the dysfunction inside the building, four people familiar with the conversation told us.
Trump was surprised when Driscoll told him how many generals and other top officers had been fired, pushed out, or passed over for promotion under Hegseth, one of the people said. Driscoll argued that the Army could not transform itself the way it needs to, because of the departure of so many leaders, this person said, adding that Trump expressed concern about the deep cuts to the Army’s senior leadership. Driscoll informed the president of his intention to resign—and by today, Driscoll was on his way out.
Hegseth’s purge of the military has been so dramatic that with Driscoll gone, the military’s largest service is left without a top civilian leader, a Senate-confirmed top general, a confirmed Army general in charge of operations, or a confirmed commander of Army troops in Europe. Because of all the firings across the service over the past year, the Army, with more than 450,000 active-duty soldiers positioned across the globe, has fewer generals than at any point in recent history. Driscoll’s personal appeal to Trump just days before his exit was the most direct articulation of high-level concerns among Pentagon leaders about the strains facing the force—including Hegseth’s intervention in Army personnel decisions and the mounting demands of the Iran war.
The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that Driscoll had been “highly effective” in improving soldier readiness and advancing other administration priorities. “The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” Kelly wrote in a statement, using the administration’s preferred term for the Department of Defense.
Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment, and Driscoll did not respond to a call seeking comment. But a person familiar with his resignation told us that Driscoll had “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible.” Hegseth did not have an immediate response to Driscoll’s departure.
[Read: The military Pete Hegseth wants]
Since his arrival at the Pentagon early last year, Hegseth—a former Fox News host who appealed to Trump loyalists by deriding a “woke” military and advocating for leniency for troops charged with war crimes—has sought to reshape the Army. He has placed like-minded generals in positions of influence, intervened to stymie the promotions of lower ranking-officers, and gutted diversity initiatives. The result was an Army depleted of leaders, and an Army secretary and a Pentagon chief at constant odds. Hegseth has ended dozens of Army careers, all without any clear explanation. He now has driven out the secretary of the Army.
Driscoll’s departure puts the Pentagon even more firmly under the control of Hegseth and his MAGA agenda. Driscoll is a confidant of Vice President Vance, a relationship that gave him access to the West Wing, and at times Driscoll served as a counterweight to Hegseth’s impulses, but only up to a point. Some current and former defense officials told us they believe Driscoll’s enmity toward Hegseth actually had the unintended consequence of broadening the purge of the uniformed ranks. And yet Driscoll’s departure, which had been expected for months, and the prospect that he will be replaced by someone more politically aligned with Hegseth are already raising fears inside the Army. “What happens then? Generational damage,” a defense official told us.
Driscoll arrived at the Pentagon in February 2025, a third-generation Army soldier who shared several things in common with Hegseth, his new boss. Like Hegseth, Driscoll joined the military in the most muscular years of Washington’s post-9/11 wars. Both men served in Iraq in a company-grade role. (Hegseth, a National Guardsman, also deployed to Afghanistan.) Both returned with sharp criticisms of America’s overseas adventures and the military’s hidebound ways. Both attended Ivy League schools: Hegseth, Princeton and Harvard; Driscoll, Yale Law, where he befriended the fellow veteran Vance. Both Driscoll and Hegseth have made unsuccessful runs for political office. Both have also eyed a return to politics. As Army secretary, Driscoll frequently reminded people that he had a direct line to the vice president, people familiar with the matter said, and told others that he had ambition to someday run for president himself—an ambition that Hegseth is also said to harbor.
But the two men differed starkly in temperament and style. Hegseth, who required an unprecedented tie-breaking Senate-confirmation vote from Vance after failing to win any Democratic support, is one of Trump’s most reliable MAGA warriors. He has publicly boasted about firing “woke” generals, dared military dissenters to quit, and demonized the mainstream media. Driscoll also supported administration policies but has done so in a more genial way that appealed to many lawmakers more than Hegseth’s combative approach before Congress. And unlike Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who has echoed Hegseth’s scornful and partisan tone on social media, Driscoll has steered clear of endorsing Hegseth’s most controversial actions or most of his culture-war priorities. Unlike Hegseth, Driscoll is friendly with the press, cultivated ties with lawmakers of both parties, and courted technology leaders as he promoted the Army’s sprint to transform how it wages war. That served him well in the administration, earning him additional responsibilities as director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and later as an unofficial mediator for the war in Ukraine. None of that sat well with Hegseth.
Army personnel appointments were a particular point of friction. Hegseth has not hesitated to push aside or promote officers as he sees fit, in many cases in ways that have irked others in the Pentagon. Driscoll advocated for General Randy George, the Army chief of staff whose name appeared on a list circulated before Trump’s return to office of senior officers who should be fired due to perceived transgressions against the MAGA agenda. Although Driscoll may have bought George time, Hegseth ultimately fired the general in April. Chris Donahue, the four-star general who headed U.S. Army Europe and Africa, followed several months later.
The Army has been without a top commander since George’s firing. General Christopher LaNeve, who was picked by Hegseth as the No. 2 officer in the Army, has been acting in that role, often going straight to Hegseth for decisions, bypassing Driscoll, according to defense officials. Hegseth is expected to nominate LaNeve to lead the Army, but Capitol Hill is already signaling that LaNeve would struggle to be confirmed, because of many lawmakers’ antipathy to Hegseth. “We are not going to reward Hegseth for what he did to the Army,” one congressional staffer told us.
[Read: Americans deserve answers from Hegseth]
The Army has long prided itself on representing the diversity of the country, but under Hegseth, minorities and women have been pushed out or barred from promotion. The military has long sought to be apolitical, but under Hegseth, troops are measured not by combat experience but by their perceived loyalty to the administration. Among the generals fired have been some of the most experienced and decorated in the service. Each departure marks the loss of decades of investment in that soldier and raises questions about how future troops can rise through the ranks.
Although Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal is expected to take over in the near term, many Pentagon officials fear that the administration will nominate the Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, another Army veteran, to replace Driscoll. Parnell, who previously made a failed bid for U.S. Senate in Pennsylvania, shares Hegseth’s pugilistic spirit and interest in culture and personnel issues. Like Hegseth, Parnell has no experience managing a large organization and would face a contentious confirmation hearing. A new Army secretary who is more politically driven—and likely less experienced and less well connected than Driscoll—could keep the service embroiled in cultural fights rather than focused on the long-term planning that Driscoll and others believe it desperately needs.
The Army secretary told Trump about problems in the Army and his friction with Hegseth, then resigned.
items.titleTR: Dan Driscoll’s Parting Shot

slots.packetSpot:
Dan Driscoll’s departure from his post as Army Secretary has brought into view reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and concerns over departures in the military’s senior ranks. It is reported that, in a White House meeting, Driscoll conveyed to President Donald Trump his concerns about the future of the military, the departures of senior commanders and Hegseth’s role in personnel decisions; he then indicated his intention to resign.

According to the accounts, Trump expressed surprise and concern over senior officers being dismissed, forced to leave or blocked from promotion. It is stated that Driscoll’s departure has left some of the military’s senior civilian and military posts without Senate-confirmed leaders. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Driscoll had been highly effective in improving troop readiness and advancing the administration’s priorities.

It is reported that Deputy Army Secretary Michael Obadal is expected to take over in the short term, while Sean Parnell is mentioned among possible successors. Driscoll’s spokesperson declined to comment; Driscoll did not respond, and Hegseth also had no immediate statement on the departure.
slots.packetTitle: Driscoll’s departure exposes Pentagon tensions

items.descriptionTR:
September is my birthday month, so this latest crop of sci-fi, fantasy, and speculative books feel especially like presents for me, but also for you! Fantasy heists, magical spy thrillers, dystopian abortionists, parallel-universe marriage stories, deepfake Dorian Grays, houses dying
￼
September is my birthday month, so this latest crop of sci-fi, fantasy, and speculative books feel especially like presents for me, but also for you! Fantasy heists, magical spy thrillers, dystopian abortionists, parallel-universe marriage stories, deepfake Dorian Grays, houses dying to be haunted—what more could you want? Let’s not forget the extra goodies from our 2026 SFF preview, Freya Marske’s Bodies of Magic and Emily St. John Mandel’s Exit Party!
*
￼
Scott Hawkins, Blacktail (Crown, September 1)
The first book in over a decade from the author of beloved modern horror cult classic The Library at Mount Char is a cause for celebration, and it also sounds weird as all get-out. The animals of the forest follow an ancient, intensely territorial hierarchy of hunters and prey: wolves versus hunting cats, half-breeds alternately accepted or spurned by their respective herds or packs. But then the humans hunt them while destroying the forest, and all those generations-long grudges go out the window as the half-wolf Blacktail rises up as the Forest God’s dark champion. On a killing spree that starts with revenge on humans but eventually approaches the apocalyptic, Blacktail encounters all manner of animal allies who want to see him bring about the end of the two-leggers’ world.
￼
Chloe Benjamin, Under Story (Putnam, September 1)
Laurel Salter, a thirtysomething scientist studying mycelium, flees her work and her broken marriage for the remote anonymity of Antarctica’s McMurdo Station. But outside the station is the Arc, an otherworldly light that draws droves of physicists—like her ex-husband, Eli—to study its effects. What he discovers confirms his theory of the antiuniverse, a parallel world where time moves backwards. But it’s Laurel who is most drawn to the antiuniverse, and the potential of healing the tragic loss that ruptured their partnership. This sounds like a speculative riff on The Last Five Years; I’m already anticipating the ugly-crying catharsis.
￼
Mary G. Thompson, Precious Children (Tachyon Publications, September 1)
This dark speculative novel could be a Black Mirror episode with its unflinching look at parents who would “do anything” to get their child back, but equally dire depiction of the privilege and entitlement that festers in such a scenario. In a future where children’s lifespans are grimly shortened, fertility clinic Generations, Inc. has a solution: wealthy families can clone their kids and circumvent death by uploading their child’s consciousness into a new host. No matter that those doubles have their own consciousnesses, not to mention foster families who have lovingly raised them. When the Blakes want the third iteration of their teenage son Geoff, young Nathan Donovan must surrender his mind for another’s—but the transfer fails, leaving both consciousnesses fighting for their survival. Meanwhile, Geoff’s sister Di comes to suspect that Geoff 2.0 was a con artist. It’s shades of old stories about missing children found who are impostors, crossed with the modern ethics of embryo donation and other fertility gray areas.
￼
Premee Mohamed, Wickhills (Tor Books, September 8)
A fantastical spy thriller set on the streets and underground passages of a magical city? Hell yes. The city of Wickhills is protected by Seaborne, an intelligence agency that hires street-smart types like Vycol Ferec on top-secret missions. But when his latest asset pickup is a scientist defecting from another city—a scientist who might be hiding an apocalyptic weapon—it burns him from Seaborne. On the run within the city that he ostensibly knows better than anyone, but that he also realizes he knows nothing about, Ferec must rearrange his entire worldview about what is right and who the “good guys” are. This also sounds like one of those novels where the setting will stick with you for a long time, from the organic quirks of Wickhill’s literal foundations to some of its centuries-old inhabitants who may hold the secrets to the city-state’s true nature.
￼
Helene Wecker, The Gates of Midnight (Harper, September 15)
Helene Wecker’s historical fantasy trilogy (that began with The Golem and the Jinni) concludes in 1930 New York City: three decades since Ahmad the jinni buried the flask containing the captured wizard Yehudah Schaalman in the Syrian desert. But when Schaalman tricks a stranger into digging up the flask, he returns to the Big Apple, intent on revenge against the golem Chava, who just wants to tend to her Brooklyn garden sanctuary in peace. Also converging upon the city are Ahmed, who has lost his job in the 1929 stock market crash, and a riveter on the under-construction Empire State Building with secret connections to all of them.
￼
S.V. Lockwood, A Complement of Scoundrels (Bindery Books, September 22)
I adore a heist, and I’m so excited to see more female-centric fantasy heists this year, between C.L. Polk’s The Feywild Job and now S.V. Lockwood’s debut. Double-crossed thief Myria sounds like a real Debbie Ocean (complimentary), in that she’s had enough time stewing in Carintheum’s jail to plot revenge on her master who put her there after cracking the Elysius Vault. Reuniting the old crew? On it. Trick the king of tricksters to get his help? She’s working that problem. Decide whether to trust a new ally when feelings are involved? This sounds like it’s going to get messy, in the best way.
￼
Alma Katsu, Incarnate (G.P. Putnam’s Sons, September 22)
A modern take on The Picture of Dorian Gray by way of social media algorithms, Alma Katsu’s latest feels very in conversation with Yesteryear: Failed influencer Dorothy Wagner decides to reinvent herself as the Dr. Frankenstein for Isabella, a stunningly realistic deepfake who quickly amasses millions of followers. But what will it mean if so many people are willing to believe that Isabella is real—will it imbue the creation with enough conviction to become dangerous to her creator? Like Frankenstein, will Isabella make the case for her own existence separate from her origins?
￼
Inez Ray, Buzzard (Bindery Books, September 22)
In 2086, corporations monitor fertility and have outlawed abortion. Midwife Mae Bastet, serving a sentence for infanticide, has spent seven years away from her children in Buzzard, the private prison run by paramilitary corporation Obsityan. Her job is ostensibly to monitor the health of teenage drone pilots, but when one of those teens becomes pregnant, it presents Mae with an awfully personal dilemma: do her duty as a midwife and risk never seeing her children again, or remain complicit with Obsityan’s crimes?
￼
Micaiah Johnson, The Unhaunting (Putnam, September 29)
From the author of The Space Between Worlds comes a horror debut that opens with a compelling premise for our times: Three lifelong best friends attempt to build a home together when one of them inherits a Civil War-era manor. Shantell is understandably skeptical of the supposedly dreamy Abernathy House that has been bequeathed to her friend Avery and his contractor brother Tobias, but those anxieties melt away when they step inside. Like, something otherworldly literally melts away the anxiety. Now, is the fact that the house itself is eerily turning them into better versions of themselves worth worrying about? Probably. Ditto the presence of ghosts from Abernathy’s construction 170 years ago, when a daughter of the Confederacy wished for a home where nothing bad would happen. Something tells me the house is tired of all that calm and wants to become something else…
items.titleTR: Antiuniverses, Deepfakes, and Clone Children: September’s Best Sci-Fi and Fantasy Books

slots.packetSpot:
The speculative fiction books announced for September 2026 form a broad selection spanning science fiction, fantasy, horror and near-future narratives. The descriptions foreground different worlds, from animals in a forest rising up against humans to a parallel universe in Antarctica where time is studied as flowing backwards; from child clones to a tale of espionage in a magical city.

The list includes books by Scott Hawkins, Chloe Benjamin, Mary G. Thompson, Premee Mohamed, Helene Wecker, S.V. Lockwood, Alma Katsu, Inez Ray and Micaiah Johnson that are scheduled for publication throughout September. The subjects also include historical fantasy set in 1930s New York, a female-centred fantasy heist, a deepfake narrative in the age of social media algorithms, a dystopian order in which abortion is banned, and a haunted mansion.
slots.packetTitle: A speculative horizon for September 2026

items.descriptionTR: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu pays for an indifferent showing in South Africa's series opener against New Zealand, as the fly-half drops to the Springbok bench.
items.titleTR: Boks drop Feinberg-Mngomezulu to bench for All Blacks rematch

items.descriptionTR: After a disappointing opening to the Greatest Rivalry series, I expect the Springboks to regroup, trust the process and beat the All Blacks in Cape Town.
items.titleTR: Beware of the wounded Springbok

slots.packetSpot:
The Springboks are preparing for Saturday's return match in Cape Town with changes to the squad after losing 33-16 to New Zealand in the opening match of the series in Johannesburg. Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has reportedly been moved to the bench, while Handre Pollard has been restored to the starting lineup at fly-half. Ethan Hooker and Cobus Reinach are reported to have entered the starting XV because of injuries to Cheslin Kolbe and Grant Williams.

Rassie Erasmus said the team created opportunities but that mistakes at critical moments proved costly; he stated that they would work during the week to be sharper in that regard. Siya Kolisi, who has recovered from a hamstring injury, is reportedly able to return, while Paul de Villiers has been named in the squad as a blindside flanker replacement in case he is not ready. Deon Fourie could also play for the first time since the 2023 Rugby World Cup final.

New Zealand are aiming to take a 2-0 lead in the four-match series. One commentary, meanwhile, expects the Springboks to recover and beat the All Blacks in Cape Town.
slots.packetTitle: The Springboks seek their footing again

items.descriptionTR:
Premier League clubs shattered their record of £3.1 billion ($4.2 billion) in transfer fees in one window on deadline day as Manchester City closed in on a £125 million deal for Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez and signed Iliman Ndiaye.But it took until the final hours before the 2200 GMT deadline for an agreement to be reportedly struck with the fee for the Argentine set to match the British transfer record that Liverpool paid for Alexander Isak on the final day of the window last year.
￼
Manchester City hope to sign Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez (Adrian DENNIS)
Premier League clubs shattered their record of £3.1 billion ($4.2 billion) in transfer fees in one window on deadline day as Manchester City closed in on a £125 million deal for Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez and signed Iliman Ndiaye.
City spearheaded a frantic final day of spending as they aim to arm Enzo Maresca with a squad capable of winning the Premier League for the first time in three seasons.
Fernandez, who previously thrived under Maresca at Chelsea, has been linked with a move to the Etihad for months.
But it took until the final hours before the 2200 GMT deadline for an agreement to be reportedly struck with the fee for the Argentine set to match the British transfer record that Liverpool paid for Alexander Isak on the final day of the window last year.
Fernandez will form a completely revamped City midfield alongside England international Elliot Anderson and Moroccan Ayyoub Bouaddi, who themselves cost over a combined £200 million.
City also added Senegal forward Ndiaye from Everton in a deal worth £65 million to bolster their forward options.
"I've worked my whole life for an opportunity like this," said Ndiaye.
"To be able to write my own chapter in a story that special is the chance of a lifetime and I'm determined to grab it with both hands."
Chelsea are aiming to replace Fernandez with Monaco's Lamine Camara.
The Blues also agreed a £40 million deal to sign 18-year-old Honest Ahanor from Atalanta from 2027, with the Italy defender spending this season on loan at Crystal Palace.
Champions Arsenal, by contrast, had a quiet deadline day after their pursuit of Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez fizzled out.
The Gunners had been rivalling Barcelona for the Argentine's signature, but the Spanish champions instead turned to Arsenal to fill their need for a forward with the signing of Gabriel Jesus.
"I had a chance 10 years ago and life took me in another direction, but now I can be here and it's a dream for me," said Jesus.
- Liverpool frustrated -
Liverpool splashed out on France forward Bradley Barcola on Monday, spending £123 million to lure him from Paris Saint-Germain.
But the Reds attempts to further add to their squad look to have been frustrated with bids for Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr and Brighton's Yankuba Minteh knocked back, meaning Cody Gakpo is set to stay despite interest from City and Tottenham.
Liverpool did complete the signing of Belgian goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans, but the 18-year-old will be loaned back to Genk for the rest of the season.
Ibrahim Mbaye was another wide player linked with a move to Anfield, but he has instead joined Aston Villa for a reported £47 million.
Mbaye played 31 times in all competitions for PSG last season as the French club won the Champions League and the Ligue 1 title.
Villa also bolstered their defence by signing Southampton centre-back Taylor Harwood-Bellis in a £29 million deal.
Tottenham are keen on a loan move for Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk after missing out on Ndiaye and Gakpo, with a £7 million swoop for his Blues team-mate Tosin Adarabioyo also lined up by the north Londoners.
Spurs have also loaned Pape Matar Sarr on a one-year deal to Juventus with an obligation to buy for a fee of 27.5 million euros ($31.9 million), should Sarr fulfil certain conditions.
City winger Jack Grealish is set to rejoin Everton on loan after his spell with David Moyes's men last season.
But Everton's pursuit of United States international Folarin Balogun is at risk of collapsing over reports the Monaco forward has failed a medical.
Newcastle landed Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille in a £51 million swoop.
The Magpies, who are rebuilding following the close-season departures of Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali, have also sent German striker Nicolas Woltemade on loan to Juventus.

items.titleTR: Man City sign Ndiaye, line up Fernandez as Premier League clubs set new spending record

slots.packetSpot: According to data provided to BBC Sport by FootballTransfers.com founder Paul Macdonald, Premier League clubs' spending during the summer transfer window reached £3.46 billion, surpassing the £3.14 billion mark from 12 months earlier. Spending of £475 million on the final day contributed to the increase. The initial payment of £60 million by Manchester City to Everton for Iliman Ndiaye, and the confirmation after the window closed of Enzo Fernandez's £125 million move from Chelsea to Manchester City, stood out. Manchester City's total spending reportedly reached £458 million, a record for a single Premier League transfer window; Liverpool's spending the previous summer was £415 million. Premier League clubs' net spending was reported to have remained above £1 billion, while 35% of fee-paying transfers reportedly took place between clubs within the league.
slots.packetTitle: Another record summer in the Premier League

items.descriptionTR: Elena Rybakina says she is "motivated" by the race to become world number one but insists her focus is on taking "one step at a time" as she got her US Open campaign off to a winning start.
items.titleTR: Rybakina makes winning start in race to number one

items.descriptionTR: Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.
items.titleTR: Injured Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball

items.descriptionTR:
•	Elena Rybakina breezes past Thea Frodin 6-3, 6-2
	•	Cobolli rallies from two sets down to beat Comesaña
On a rainy afternoon in New York filled with frustrating delays for the majority of players waiting to enter the court for the first-round matches at the US Open, Madison Keys took advantage of her prime court assignment under the Arthur Ashe Stadium roof by closing out Alina Korneeva 7-5, 6-4 to reach the second round.
This year marks a milestone 15th US Open appearance for the 31‑year‑old Keys, who turned professional on her 14th birthday in February 2009. The 2025 Australian Open singles champion has spent her recent days reflecting on the fact that she has now officially worked as a tennis player for the majority of her life.
items.titleTR: Madison Keys beats nerves and Alina Korneeva to progress at US Open

slots.packetSpot:
As first-round results at the US Open in New York clarify who has advanced to the second round, Thanasi Kokkinakis withdrew before his match against Rafael Jodar because of an ankle sprain. Kokkinakis said it may be his final US Open.

Elena Rybakina advanced to the second round by beating 17-year-old wild card Thea Frodin 6-3 and 6-2. items.descriptionTR:
What Ole Miss football QB Trinidad Chambliss said about being compared to ex-NFL players in college such as Dae'Quan Wright
OXFORD — Ole Miss football quarterback Trinidad Chambliss has noticed he's been dragged into discussions online regarding a former teammate who is attempting a return to college football.
Former Ole Miss tight end Dae'Quan Wright has made headlines for his return to college football in 2026. Wright started for Ole Miss in 2025 and entered the 2026 NFL Draft.
After going undrafted, Wright signed with the Philadelphia Eagles. He was cut and signed another deal with the Cleveland Browns. After a court order gave Wright eligibility to return to college football, he entered the transfer portal, transferred to LSU and practiced with the Tigers on Aug. 31.
Chambliss was asked about Wright's move in a press conference on Sept. 1 ahead of No. 10 Ole Miss' Week 1 game against Louisville in Nashville (6:30 p.m. CT, ABC).
"I've seen it on social media and stuff, but that's not where my attention is right now," Chambliss said. "I'm really not worried about that. Just worried about Louisville and making sure our team is in the best position possible to be successful out there."
Chambliss, 24, also fought for his eligibility in 2026 by suing the NCAA. Chambliss argued a should receive a medical hardship waiver because he has played just three complete seasons. He was awarded a temporary injunction against the NCAA in February, clearing his path to play in 2026.
The big difference in Chambliss' case is he never played professional football. He has still drawn criticism for seeking to return to college instead of entering the 2026 NFL Draft.
Chambliss is older than Wright, who turns 23 on Sept. 21.
"People are going to say what they want to say," Chambliss said. "They are always going to have a narrative and an opinion about you. I really don't give that any mind. Don't really think about that. Because at the end of the day the only thing that matters is what I think and what my team thinks."
Sam Hutchens covers Ole Miss for the Clarion Ledger. Email him at Shutchens@gannett.com or reach him on X at @Sam_Hutchens_
This article originally appeared on Mississippi Clarion Ledger: Ole Miss' Trinidad Chambliss reacts to his return called same as Dae'Quan Wright's
items.titleTR: Ole Miss' Trinidad Chambliss reacts to his return called same as Dae'Quan Wright's

slots.packetSpot:
The eligibility debate in college football is growing through two distinct cases. Dae’Quan Wright, who briefly signed a contract in the NFL, has been taking part in practices with LSU following a court ruling, while whether he can take the field still depends on the judge’s decision. Clemson head coach Dabo Swinney described the situation as “embarrassing,” while Colts general manager Chris Ballard opposed the idea of NFL players returning to college.

Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss’s situation is different: Chambliss, who has not played professional football, obtained a temporary restraining order in his lawsuit against the NCAA over a request for a medical hardship waiver. Despite comparisons with Wright, he said his own focus is his team’s success.

At the center of the debate is not only who can return to college football, but also how court rulings and the NFL’s contract, roster and draft consequences will shape that path.

As the French government begins work on the 2027 Finance Bill, weak growth, rising borrowing costs and spending commitments are narrowing fiscal room. Sébastien Lecornu is seeking opposition support for the bill expected to be presented at the end of September; he is proposing an interim “first-half budget” that could be amended by the majority formed after the presidential election.

There is a risk that the public deficit will exceed the target of 5% of gross domestic product. items.titleTR: The election campaign to replace Macron in France is heating up as the summer vacation season ends

slots.packetSpot:
In France, where Emmanuel Macron is constitutionally barred from running for a third consecutive term, the presidential race is entering a more active phase with the end of the summer recess. While 18 April has been set for the first round and 2 May for the second, Marine Le Pen is reported to be leading in voting-intention polls for both rounds.

More than 20 people are said to have announced their candidacy or to be considering one; Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure is the latest to join them. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, former Macron-era prime ministers Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau, Raphaël Glucksmann and Marine Tondelier are listed among the prominent potential rivals. A debate attended by seven potential candidates at Roland Garros in Paris is presented as the unofficial starting signal for the campaign.

While polls indicate that Le Pen could be one of the candidates to reach the second round, the main uncertainty is who will face her. It is assessed that a fragmented field could work in Le Pen’s favour. In an interview with Anthony Lattier, Jean-Yves Dormagen, president of Cluster 17 and a professor of political science, also examines the foundations of Le Pen’s unusual advantage in the first and second rounds and the framework of the campaign now under way.

Le Pen is reported to have been cleared to run a new presidential campaign by a Paris appeals court ruling that shortened the ban on standing for election imposed by a lower court in connection with an embezzlement case. The race is unfolding at a time of pressures including a stagnant economy, rising energy costs, the war in Ukraine, uncertainties over the transatlantic alliance, competition with China, artificial intelligence and public debt.
