items.descriptionTR:
Tensions between Washington and Ottawa are at a steady simmer, with no sign of de-escalation.
The U.S.-Canada trade standoff is threatening to stretch past the midterm elections. The White House is shrugging off the threat.
With a week to go before Canada imposes its retaliatory tariffs — aimed at key industries in states like Ohio and Texas with competitive Senate elections — tensions between Washington and Ottawa are at a steady simmer, with no sign of de-escalation.
Trump administration officials are united in the posture that the U.S. has the upper hand in the trade war, and risks exponentially less economic fallout than Canada. And they are signaling that the Canadian government, led by Prime Minister Mark Carney, will have to be the one to offer concessions to restart talks.
Privately, Trump officials are telling industry groups that the offer Canadian negotiators rejected on Aug. 21 is now moot, and they are no longer willing to make the same concessions on steel and aluminum tariffs, in particular.
The Canadians, meanwhile, have drawn a red line at key U.S. demands, like maintaining a 25 percent tariff on medium and heavy duty trucks. And Carney’s decision to stand up to Trump after months of rhetorical attacks and threats have helped produce a surge of Canadian patriotism and support for his Liberal Party, evidenced by their clean sweep of three special by-elections Monday.
The prime minister has little reason to back down ahead of votes in October in two provinces with strong separatist factions, who could challenge his political coalition.
As a result, both governments are digging in and readying for a longer trade war, all but guaranteeing the standoff bleeds into the fall campaign season.
Asked how Washington and Ottawa can find their way back to the table, a person familiar with the talks said, “You’ve got to get past the local elections in Canada.”
In the U.S., many Republicans fear the trade war will cut the other way, hurting the president’s party in the November congressional elections. House Republicans requested a meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer later this week to discuss Trump’s new tariffs on Canada, amid rising unease in Congress.
The White House doesn’t believe the tariff tit-for-tat with Canada will really be a factor in the elections, however. Greer argued in an interview Monday with POLITICO Playbook that the duties are too small to move the U.S. economy, adding they are “more [Canada’s] emergency than ours.”
But polls show Trump’s trade policies are increasingly unpopular, and Democrats are determined to make them an issue over the next two months, particularly in border states with economies that are tightly intertwined with their Canadian neighbors’. Michigan Democrats launched new attacks Monday on Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers for refusing to denounce the tariffs, with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed calling Trump an “asshole” for launching the trade war.
“They’re very damaging politically,” said Mike Madrid, a Republican strategist and vocal Trump critic, referring to Trump’s tariffs. “They’re hurting his base vote and the voters that he needs the most.”
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
There is still plenty of time between now and November, however, for negotiators to return to the table. Carney’s “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation goes into effect on Sept. 8 and Trump’s counter-counter measure — a threatened 50 percent tariffs on autos and auto parts — won’t go into effect until New Year’s Day, a sign both sides want to give space to negotiate a future truce.
And despite Trump’s weekend Truth Social tirade against Canada and his decision last week to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” the president has shown a willingness to back down from his threats when presented with a good deal.
“Four months is, as you know, like an eternity for this president on tariffs. And so he gave them a lot of runway here to make their way back,” said one trade lobbyist, granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive talks.
In Ottawa, the political boost Carney is enjoying for standing up to Trump and pulling his negotiators out of talks last month will likely start to ebb as the economic impacts of the trade war deepen.
The tariffs Trump imposed on Canada hit $20 billion worth of imports, only about 5 percent of what the U.S. imports from Canada annually. Canada’s tariffs on the US, likewise, hit the same value. But the figure lands far harder north of the border, since the U.S. takes nearly three-quarters of Canada’s exports.
Given the economic risk, U.S. officials believe Carny has another, non-economic motive — using the tension with the U.S. to influence two key votes in October. In Alberta, home to Calgary, voters will decide on Oct. 19 whether to hold a referendum to secede from Canada. In Quebec, the secessionist party, Parti Quebecois, is in prime position to gain seats in the province’s legislative body on Oct. 8.
In one of Monday’s special by-elections, however, the candidate from Carney’s Liberal party edged out a Quebec separatist in a district hit hard by U.S. tariffs, giving the prime minister and his government new confidence ahead of the fall votes.
Separatist leader of the Parti Québécois Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, meanwhile, has vowed to not hold a referendum until Trump has left office to protect the issue from being “hijacked by the ups and downs of American politics.”
“Carney walked away for a reason,” said the trade lobbyist. “He’s going to continue to try to take advantage of this politically before maybe the concern about that very significant kind of ratcheting up of the economic pain on steel and autos could force him back to the table.”
Quebec’s French heritage has already emerged as a key sticking point in the trade negotiations with the U.S., with Carney’s government suggesting the U.S. tried to force Canada to back off a law that would require streaming platforms to promote French-language content in Canada.
Greer disputed that, saying the issue was really about Canada imposing its own regulations on U.S. companies and told the CBC “there is no way we would let a good deal go by for something like this.”
Canadian Minister for Trade with the U.S. Dominic LeBlanc said he “welcomed” the U.S. “withdrawing” its position on French language and culture requirements.
And Carney told reporters in Ottawa Tuesday morning that he viewed the offer the Trump administration made in August to lower some of its tariffs in exchange for trade concessions in Canada as unfinished work, not a done deal. “There were elements of that mutually beneficial deal that we were moving towards, which is why we were still at the table. But we never viewed that we had that deal, and it diverged towards the end,” Carney said.
“In my way of looking at it, both sides have opened the crack in the door to get back to the negotiating table,” said David Cohen, the U.S. ambassador to Canada under former President Joe Biden.
But the U.S. has also been clear that the original deal is now off the table — including a proposal to lower some metal tariffs from 50 percent to 25 percent, according to two people close to the administration, who were granted anonymity to discuss details that have not been made public. The domestic metals sector lobbied hard against that part of the tentative deal Trump announced on Aug. 18 — blowback that contributed to the deal unraveling days later.
In the meantime, Trump has continued to hammer the Canadians on Truth Social and in media appearances, suggesting the country has “ripped off” the U.S. for years.
Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association President Flavio Volpe, a member of Carney’s Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, predicted there would be more of that rhetoric before the two countries can restart talks.
“The [Trump] administration will need to get its Canada bashing campaign out of its system first,” Volpe said.
Carney echoed that in his remarks in Ottawa Tuesday, while adding that a mutually beneficial trade deal is still possible. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions.”
Megan Messerly contributed reporting to this article.

items.descriptionTR:
The Latin American country is negotiating its tariff terms while navigating the uncertain future of the USMCA trade agreement
The partners of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) are in crisis. The U.S. and Canada have escalated their trade war in recent days, imposing mutual tariffs and casting uncertainty over negotiations about the future of the pact they share with Mexico. The Latin American country has not been part of the convoluted talks, but it is on edge about how the tension between Washington and Ottawa could affect its own negotiations with the Trump administration and, ultimately, the economic impact of the Republican president’s feud with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has avoided going into detail about the rupture between the United States and Canada, but she sent Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard to Washington on an emergency basis. “I am optimistic that an agreement can be reached,” the president said at her Monday press conference.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Mexico watches US–Canada trade tension with uncertainty

slots.packetSpot:
As the tariff standoff between Washington and Ottawa continues, negotiations are reported to have frozen, with no resolution in sight in the near term. In response to US tariffs on Canadian-origin steel, aluminum, lumber, automobiles and other products, Canada announced “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs expected to take effect on September 8.

Assessments that the economic burden will not be distributed evenly are coming to the fore: manufacturing sectors in Ontario and Quebec, along with US states such as Ohio, Illinois and Pennsylvania, are seen as particularly exposed. Canada is estimated to have lost 55,000 manufacturing jobs from the start of 2025 to the start of 2026; if the new US tariffs persist, the total loss could reach 90,000. In the US, meanwhile, Trump’s tariffs on various countries are calculated to be able to create an average additional cost of $840 per household this year.

The tension is turning into a political test on both sides of the border. While Mark Carney’s stance against Trump is reported to have increased support for the Liberal Party in Canada, some Republicans in the US are said to be concerned about the tariffs ahead of congressional elections. Uncertainty over the future of the USMCA continues, while Mexico supports renewing the agreement; contacts led by Claudia Sheinbaum and Marcelo Ebrard are being conducted separately with Washington. Nevertheless, it is also stated that the reciprocal steps still leave room for negotiations.
slots.packetTitle: North America’s tightening trade fault line

items.descriptionTR:
Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars
For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country.
Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves.
items.titleTR: Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaign

items.descriptionTR:
The Trump administration’s trade and financial squeeze has hurt Tehran, but it has not toppled the regime’s productive backbone while civilians bear the brunt
“An economic D-Day.” Donald Trump’s vocabulary is as narrow as it is hyperbolic. But his threat, issued Wednesday, falls into a new category. Referring to June 6, 1944 — the day of the Normandy landings that changed the course of modern history — the U.S. president warned that Iran was facing “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country.” Yet, nearly six months into the U.S. offensive against Tehran, its economy, though damaged, is far from derailed: if any society is used to coping with decades of sanctions and autarky, it is the Islamic Republic.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: After six months of war, Washington has failed to strangle Iran’s economy

items.descriptionTR: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday said Iran’s economy could collapse “within weeks or months,” as the Trump administration seeks to debilitate the Middle Eastern country’s economy. “I think it could be within weeks or months –– and the economy doesn’t have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses,”…
items.titleTR: Bessent: Iran economy could collapse ‘within weeks or months’

slots.packetSpot:
The Trump administration is increasing sanctions pressure on Iran with new financial measures and warnings aimed at trade channels in third countries. While US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicts that the economy could collapse within weeks or months, Iran’s economy, which has adapted to sanctions for years, is reported to continue functioning despite severe damage.

It is stated that data on Iran’s economy are limited and their reliability is disputed. According to World Bank data, GDP contracted by 2.7 percent in the March 2025–March 2026 period; the IMF projected a contraction of 6.1 percent for the current year, then 5.4 percent, citing better-than-expected oil exports and certain relaxations in export restrictions. Annual inflation is reported to have exceeded 80 percent, food prices to have risen by more than double over the past 12 months, and the loss of purchasing power to have hit households in particular.

Under the campaign Washington calls “Operation Economic Outcast,” five Banque Misr branches in the UAE proposed for removal from the US correspondent banking system, along with the Bank Melli branch manager in Dubai and a Hong Kong-based trading company, stand out. The UAE’s suspension of trade and financial ties with Iran is seen as an additional source of pressure whose consequences cannot yet be foreseen. Commercial vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz are also reported to have fallen sharply; war-risk insurance costs have risen, and seafarers have been left stranded aboard ships.

The political consequences of the pressure remain uncertain. While some assessments in Tehran indicate that sanctions could erode production capacity over time, the networks Iran has established to circumvent oil sanctions, import substitution and relative adequacy in staple foods leave open the question of how long the economy can endure.
slots.packetTitle: Iran’s economic breaking point

items.descriptionTR: New research on remote work resistance argues that some leaders do not simply prefer the office because collaboration is easier there — they prefer it because the office gives them an audience, a hierarchy and a stage.
items.titleTR: When a return-to-office mandate is just about the boss’s narcissism

slots.packetSpot:
Six years after the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift to remote work, remote and hybrid arrangements have become an established part of Canada’s labour market. About one-fifth of Canadians are reported to work remotely all or part of the time.

This shift brings to the fore the question of what being in the office is for. While the costs of remote arrangements in terms of learning opportunities for younger workers are being debated, it is suggested that resistance to remote work may be driven not only by a need for collaboration but also by a pursuit of power and authority. Research indicates that leaders with higher narcissistic personality traits are more strongly opposed to remote and hybrid work, and that power motivation plays a role in this pattern. This does not mean that every advocate of the office is narcissistic or that every return-to-work mandate is imposed for the same reason.
slots.packetTitle: The office finds a new purpose

items.descriptionTR:
China and Australia drove global decline in new capacity additions in 2025, but planned production kept growing
The post New coal mine openings slow as East Asian demand plateaus appeared first on Climate Home News.
The world saw the lowest amount of new coal mine capacity brought online for at least 10 years in 2025, according to a new report, as clean energy displaces coal for electricity generation in East Asia.
A report by Global Energy Monitor (GEM) found that new coal mine capacity declined by nearly 40% from 2024, the second consecutive year new mine capacity has hit a decade low. This represents an acceleration of a steady decline that began in 2019.
The slowdown in new coal mine openings was driven by China and Australia, where new additions fell by 44% and 96%, respectively. In China, the report said this was partly due to solar and wind displacing coal for electricity generation – although coal rebounded in the first half of 2026 – and the National Energy Administration implementing new rules to curb new mine openings.

In Australia, a 96% reduction in new coal mine capacity was driven by shrinking demand from the countries that import Australian coal for electricity, like Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, the report said.
This trend is likely to continue, according to GEM, as the Australian state of New South Wales recently banned new coal mines on undeveloped greenfield land. South Korea has promised to stop building coal-fired power plants that cannot capture and store the emissions produced. Meanwhile, Japan is pushing for a post-Fukushima nuclear revival to displace coal.
This Australian coal community is co-designing its own green future
Globally, growth in coal demand has slowed over the last few years and the International Energy Agency expects it to plateau through to 2030 because of increases in renewable energy, nuclear and fossil gas.
Openings down, pipeline up
But while new coal mine openings fell, the amount of global coal mine capacity proposed increased by 11%. This was almost entirely driven by a spate of projects in the eastern Indian states of Jharkhand and Odisha.
“If built,” the GEM report says, “the projects would commit India – a country with no formal coal phaseout timeline – to years of coal expansion and would put a 1.5C-aligned transition away from fossil fuels farther out of reach”.
The Indian government says it needs to increase coal production to meet growing electricity demand from economic growth and from dealing with heatwaves. It plans to open more than 20 new coal mines to meet its coal production targets.
Because of energy security concerns, India is also aiming to produce chemicals with Indian coal rather than imported gas. China is also pursuing this strategy, although the Global Energy Monitor report said that Indian coal’s high ash content means the South Asian nation will find it harder to make chemicals from coal.
	•	￼   Jun 22, 2026  Comment   China’s coal-chemicals boom risks repeating the mistakes of the past By reviving the problematic industry in the name of energy security, China runs the risk of higher emissions, stranded assets and setting back its ambitions as a clean energy leader  Read more    
	•	￼   Aug 11, 2026  Oceans   South Africa’s offshore oil push meets grassroots resistance in court Two court cases against oil majors TotalEnergies and Shell could derail South Africa’s plan to expand offshore fossil fuels  Read more    
	•	￼   Aug 6, 2026  News   Quarter of countries still missing UN climate plans 18 months after deadline Egypt, Vietnam, Argentina and the Philippines are among the 45 nations that have breached the Paris Agreement by not submitting a new NDC to the UN  Read more    
	•	
Nations agreed at COP26 five years ago to “phase down” coal power – a commitment that China and India successfully pushed to weaken from “phase out”. At COP28 in 2023, governments agreed to transition away from all fossil fuels in energy systems.
Since then, wealthy nations have partnered with coal-producing countries like South Africa, Vietnam and Indonesia on plans to transition from coal to clean energy. But, after preliminary talks, India and these donor governments did not agree a JETP.
items.titleTR: New coal mine openings slow as East Asian demand plateaus

slots.packetSpot:
According to Global Energy Monitor (GEM), new coal mine capacity commissioned in 2025 fell to its lowest level in at least a decade, with China and Australia decisive in the decline. By contrast, plans to expand aluminium production in Indonesia rely on coal-fired facilities, while proposed new mining projects in India are pushing capacity higher.

GEM reports that new mine capacity fell by about 40 percent compared with 2024, declining by 44 percent in China and 96 percent in Australia. The organisation also says proposed global mine capacity rose by 11 percent, driven by projects in the Indian states of Jharkhand and Odisha. The International Energy Agency expects global coal demand to remain flat through 2030 because of growth in renewable energy, nuclear power and fossil gas.

According to the Associated Press, Indonesia aims to increase aluminium production from about 1 million tonnes in 2025 to 14.5 million tonnes in 2030, while raising alumina production to 32.5 million tonnes. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) is tracking 32 off-grid coal power plants planned to be built by private companies to supply electricity to aluminium smelters. Chinese companies are reported to have invested in about three-quarters of the planned Indonesian projects; CREA is reported to put Chinese investment at between $5.5 billion and $6 billion and to project that it could rise to $30 billion by 2030.

The expansion in Indonesia is gaining momentum after disruptions to aluminium supply in the Middle East during the Iran war, according to the Associated Press. Environmental advocates, meanwhile, are voicing concern about the emissions, air pollution and effects on local communities of these coal-fired facilities.
slots.packetTitle: Coal's uneven retreat across Asia

superPackets.axis: The renewed U.S.–Iran confrontation, encompassing fighting, economic pressure, diplomacy, shipping and energy exposure, market reactions, and legal accountability ← Renewed U.S.–Iran fighting and explicitly linked fallout: truce pressure, Hormuz shipping risks, energy and export disruption, market shocks, and wartime legal accountability ⊕ ABD’nin İran’ı ekonomik olarak sıkıştırma kampanyası ve Çin’in bu kampanyadaki başlıca gedik olması
superPackets.body: US Central Command linked the initial strikes on Larak Island to an observation that Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were preparing to launch rockets carrying mines into the Strait of Hormuz; it presented the subsequent broader strikes as a response to recent attempts against commercial ships and US personnel in the region. Iran attacked US targets in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates; President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran would respond in kind if Washington returned to an agreement, while Donald Trump threatened heavier attacks. Maritime intelligence and tracking firms Marisks and Kpler reported that two tankers carrying 2 million barrels of Saudi crude each were struck minutes apart in Hormuz by unidentified munitions; the IMF PortWatch seven-day average for the week ending 23 August showed tanker transits at five. The Straits Times wrote that, under a US naval blockade, Iran had not shipped meaningful volumes of crude through Hormuz for about seven weeks; Kpler data cited by The National showed departures from Kharg falling from 1.98 million barrels a day in February to 135,000 barrels a day in August. By contrast, Lin Ye of Rystad Energy, who saw the Larak strike’s direct effect on exports as limited, described the price rise as markets pricing in the risk of escalation and retaliation; Brent rose by as much as 3% on Monday, while by Tuesday’s close oil had reached its highest level in about six weeks and European gas its highest since 2023. France 24 noted that oil rose, shares fell and bond yields jumped after the attacks; Bloomberg and Euronews reported these moves alongside multiple factors including Middle East tensions, inflation concerns and a possible US interest-rate increase. On a separate track, Washington expanded the scope of secondary sanctions under the name “Operation Economic Outcast”; the European Union announced its support for economic pressure, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that the sanctions were intended to create conditions that would bring Iran to the negotiating table and that Iran had responded militarily because of economic losses. NPR described China as the plan’s “big hole,” basing that characterisation on Beijing’s statement that it would not join the campaign, Chinese independent refiners’ purchases of discounted Iranian oil, and Washington’s failure so far to sanction Chinese financial institutions. The Guardian placed the new campaign alongside rising food prices, closed petrol stations and foreign-currency shortages; Deutsche Welle linked fuel queues to war damage, import restrictions and sanctions, but these outlets did not present the renewed conflict as a measured result of the economic campaign. In the legal sphere, Melanie O’Brien, writing in The Conversation, argued that the US attacks and threats against civilian facilities should be investigated and that some actions could constitute war crimes; the record contained no court ruling on these claims, no independently measured causality between the renewed attacks and the economic campaign, or any conclusion on the fate of the ceasefire.
superPackets.title: The knot in the strait

superPackets.axis: Escalating U.S.–Canada friction expressed through tariffs and the proposed renaming of Lake Ontario ← ABD-Kanada arasındaki tırmanan ve uzaması beklenen ticaret savaşı ile tarife gerilimi ⊕ Trump’ın Ontario Gölü’nü “Lake America” olarak yeniden adlandırma girişimi ve buna verilen kurumsal ve siyasi tepkiler
superPackets.body:
US tariffs on $20 billion of imports from Canada are in force; Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” tariffs on US goods of the same value will begin on September 8. Trump’s announcement of 50 percent tariffs on automobiles and auto parts remained a threat aimed at the new year. POLITICO wrote that the two governments were preparing for a longer conflict; while US officials said the previous offer was no longer valid, Mark Carney described the August talks as unfinished work and said a mutually beneficial agreement was still possible. Carney also called on US officials to “get serious”; while Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she was optimistic that an agreement could be reached, El País wrote that the tension had created uncertainty over the future of the USMCA.

During the same period of record, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to use the name “Lake America” for Lake Ontario; Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Trump had appealed directly to Apple for the change. Google and Apple began using the new label on their maps in the United States; Lake Ontario remained in Canadian versions, while international versions displayed both names together. While official federal maps had not yet been updated, Google cited its established policy of following Geographic Names Information System data. MapQuest announced that it would not change the name and rose to first place in the US Apple App Store download rankings; no measurement was recorded as to how long that rise would last. Democratic Representative Tim Kennedy and two colleagues introduced the Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act, aimed at blocking the change.

POLITICO, The Guardian, Ars Technica, The Verge and The National recorded the naming in the same context as the trade dispute; no source recorded that this was a coordinated strategy encompassing the two disputes.
superPackets.title: A name on the map, a tariff at the border

superPackets.axis: Russia’s war in Ukraine as observed through attacks on infrastructure and European opposition to Russian participation in G20 finance talks ← European opposition to Russia’s participation in G20 finance talks ⊕ Rusya’nın Ukrayna’daki sivil ve ekonomik altyapıyı hedef alan güncel saldırıları
superPackets.body:
Ukrainian officials reported that at least 12 people were killed and many others, including three children, were injured in attacks on Kyiv and its surroundings on 1 September; earlier reports had put the death toll at nine. Ukrainian state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said six employees were killed when a ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot and that other railway facilities were also hit; while the Guardian described the attacks as the deliberate targeting of the rail network, the material provided contained no independent confirmation of the damage or Russian statement regarding those targets. In separate reports, Ukrainian officials said port infrastructure in the Odesa region and a crossing on the Romanian border were hit; NPR noted that shelves in some Kyiv markets were left empty after repeated attacks on warehouses.

At the G20 finance meeting in Asheville, Germany and other European financial officials objected to the United States inviting Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov; The Hill reported that those officials said Siluanov’s participation risked normalising relations with Moscow while Russia continues its full-scale war against Ukraine. RFI and Deutsche Welle also wrote that Russia’s return to the meetings had prompted a backlash in Europe; the records presented contain no indication that European actors removed Siluanov from the meeting or that the G20 changed Russia’s participation. No source recorded that the latest attacks in Kyiv and Odesa prompted the objections in Asheville.
superPackets.title: Two fronts of war: Kyiv's skies, Asheville's table

superPackets.axis: John Ternus succeeding Tim Cook as Apple CEO and using his first staff note to signal a major product launch ← John Ternus’un Tim Cook’un ardından Apple CEO’luğunu devralması ve CEO olarak ilk personel notunda yaklaşan büyük ürün lansmanını duyurması
superPackets.body: John Ternus became Apple CEO on 1 September, replacing Tim Cook after 15 years; Cook remained at Apple as chairman of the board. In Cook’s final email to employees, quoted by The National, Cook wrote: “Few people understand what it takes to make world-changing products the way John does.” A Bloomberg report carried by The Verge and TechCrunch said that, in his first staff note, Ternus thanked Cook and told employees: “Next week we have a massive launch that is going to be huge. Thank you all for what you do to make this possible.” He also referred to “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even dreamed of yet.” The Verge and TechCrunch presented those remarks alongside Apple’s 9 September event and expectations or rumours concerning new iPhones, including a foldable model; the note itself did not name a product, offer launch details beyond the phrase “next week,” measure its significance, or explain whether Ternus intended strategic continuity with Cook’s tenure or a departure from it.
superPackets.title: The opening scene of Apple’s handover

superPackets.axis: US Open early-round results and draw developments through the third day ← US Open’ın ilk tur ve üçüncü güne uzanan erken tur sonuçları ile kura gelişmeleri
superPackets.body: In the first round, Mariano Navone beat Novak Djokovic in five sets, leading to Djokovic's earliest Grand Slam exit in 20 years; while ABC Australia and The Athletic highlighted the result, the BBC focused on uncertainty over Djokovic's future after the defeat. In his first singles match after more than four months, Carlos Alcaraz overcame Roman Safiullin in three sets and was drawn against Jaime Faria in the second round; Stefanos Tsitsipas eliminated 10th seed Arthur Fils, while Andrey Rublev progressed in five sets after saving a match point. Aryna Sabalenka, Iga Swiatek, Amanda Anisimova, Naomi Osaka, Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova won their opening matches, while The National tracked these results alongside Fils's elimination; the Guardian's day-three record included the wins of Elena Rybakina and Madison Keys, as well as the still ongoing schedule involving Coco Gauff and Arthur Fery. The BBC highlighted Rybakina's own explanation of her motivation in the race to become world number one; the Guardian recorded Rybakina's 6-3, 6-2 win over Thea Frodin, Keys's 7-5, 6-4 victory over Alina Korneeva, and Flavio Cobolli's comeback from two sets down. Thanasi Kokkinakis withdrew before playing because of injury; ABC Australia relayed his remarks that this could be his final US Open. The eliminations of Djokovic and Fils, and Kokkinakis's withdrawal, changed the relevant sections of the draw, but no outlet recorded that these changes brought any of the remaining players closer to winning the tournament; nor did the coverage include completed results for the Gauff and Fery matches on the day-three schedule.
superPackets.title: New paths through an opening draw

superPackets.axis: Forecasts of a very strong El Niño and effects anticipated or already reported across regions ← Çok güçlü El Niño tahminleri ile farklı bölgelerde beklenen veya şimdiden görülen etkileri
superPackets.body: Forecasts issued for South Africa indicated that the developing El Niño could be very strong through the summer and could peak between October and January, while experts said the regional consequences were not certain; the South African Weather Service described the 2026-2027 event as “exceptionally strong,” warning that severe heatwaves, water shortages and hotter, drier conditions could emerge. In the United Kingdom, Kew experts said autumn winds associated with El Niño could lead to widespread tree deaths among trees made vulnerable by the summer’s extreme heat and drought; no figure was given for this effect. While noting that months remained until the event’s peak, CBC presented seabirds, siltation, salt and preparedness efforts as “early impacts,” but no separate measure of causality for each of these was included. The WMO’s outlook at the end of July projected that the event would become “strong” by October and increase the risk of above-normal temperatures and disrupted rainfall across much of the world; António Guterres carried this into a public warning framed around seasonal records and more severe global impacts. The same report relayed separate attribution studies on human-caused climate change for European fires, while an unnamed WMO scientist was cited as saying that El Niño’s global effects had not yet fully taken hold. A millennium-long coral reconstruction reported by Ars Technica showed recent El Niño oscillations to be unusually strong in their historical context; researchers said the models did not agree with one another and that the observational record was too short to distinguish whether global warming is strengthening ENSO. No source stated that the forecast final intensity had materialised or that the outcomes listed for South Africa, the United Kingdom and other regions had become certain.
superPackets.title: El Niño rides atop a warming world
